title_x: Content Creation and a Bit o' Gaming
text:
It’s the latest FusionTech ABC (a ABC 17 9720), and as such it does merit a bit of discussion as to what this laptop is intended to do. So spoiler warning….

This is NOT a gaming laptop. Oh sure, it’s easy to look at the specs and conclude that it would do great in that space, but in all honesty…while it can acquit itself reasonably well in the gaming space, it’s not really what it’s designed to do. Think of a car like a Mercedes S580…fantastic car, big twin turbo engine…but it’s not the kind of car I’d take on a rally. This FusionTech is along the same lines…the machine itself is fast, but it’s not designed around gaming (more on these specifics in a minute).

No, this is a machine with a focus on content creation. The 17” screen (itself a rarity in the laptop world) with its 16:10 dimensions (yep, 16:10) is the first clue. And really…it’s a breathtaking display, with 3840x2400 resolution and fantastic color reproduction. Brightness is also fantastic, itself a welcome sight (heh) in a laptop. It’s a display that really does eclipse the hardware (again, more on that in a minute). This all said, very minor criticism with the refresh rate being 60 Hz, however that’s not really a sin in the content creation world…

Moreover, this 17" screen has extremely thin bezels which, combined with the 16:10 ratio, somehow fits into a package with the dimensions of a 15" laptop. I frankly marvel at the sorcery involved here.

Graphics, sure you have the onboard Intel graphics, but there’s a discrete NVIDIA RTX 3050 there too. And this bears mention. While it’s a capable GPU, in this application its…well, the implementation and tuning is more for photo work than gaming. The NVIDIA control panel suggests this card is limited to a TGP ceiling of about 65W, whereas gaming-focused laptops shoot for a ceiling of around 80W. What this means is that raw graphics processing performance is not suited for AAA games. It CAN, along with the other internals, boost for a short time before thermal limitations make a system slowdown necessary.

This laptop uses DDR5 SODIMMs, with architecture support for up to 64GB. The laptop in this listing ships with 16GB, which is in my opinion a bit low. Frankly, for a content creation machine (photo/video editing, etc), in my opinion there isn’t such a thing as too much RAM. Max this thing out. 16GB is entry level at best, and when working with a lot of Photoshop layers is inadequate. I will mention that FusionTech is a little protective when it comes to memory upgrades, so RAM with overclocking profiles is out. I've upgraded to 64GB Crucial RAM (regular, not their Impact gaming line) to good effect.

Storage is in the form of a 500GB SSD (Gen 4!!!) which again on paper seems spare. But is it? For photo editing I’m more likely to be pulling RAW files directly off of memory cards, using an external SSD, and my working files are managed by the Adobe Creative Cloud. However, there is a second PCIe NVMe slot available to add another SSD, so the flexibility for more local storage does exist. These are Gen 4 slots, so go nuts. Adding a Gen 4 2TB SSD was trivial and indeed with Lightroom Classic is a reasonable way to go. Heat sinks for both slots are provided. (Quick update - Gen 4 SSDs create a lot of heat under continued use, and performance drops off with the heat. The included heatsinks offers marginally better performance, but for my use case I replaced one with a 2mm heatsink with vanes...so takeaway, if you go the Gen 4 route and have lots of data read/writes I really suggest buying some aftermarket heat sinks.).

The design is another hint as to the purpose of this machine. It’s thin, made of metal, and carries a definite Mac vibe to it. That thin profile does have implications…it isn’t as efficient with the thermals as a thick(er) gaming laptop case with cooling pipes all over the place would be. But it’s beautiful and given that this machine excels at Photoshop, very appropriate. Keyboard is very good for the genre here, and the trackpad is roughly the size of a hockey rink.

See, the thing is that at a computer at this price point, it's going to do one thing extremely well and other things merely competently. In other words, while the price for this computer is up there, it’s important to understand that this money is NOT buying top tier gaming performance. It’s buying an excellent display and a system tailored to create stuff. It does seem a bit curious that there’s such a gorgeous UHD+ screen attached to a RTX 3050. The way the GPU is tuned in this laptop, the sweet spot for this configuration seems to be at 1080p and indeed for most of my photo/video efforts on this laptop I’ve kept it right at that resolution. True, it can show higher resolutions, but in practice 1080p at 60 hz is just fine.

Ports: This is a modern laptop. USB-C Thunderbolt 4 is the dominant (and only...) port, along with a SD card reader and audio jack. USB-C is also used for charging the laptop. There’s a point that it could use more ports, there’s also a point that a hub is a reasonable solution, esp for a creation laptop that may need some versatility in connections to cameras and such. On the very plus side, the USB-C supports DisplayPort which (through a powered hub) means I can use VR.

The wifi merits a mention. It doesn’t support 6E. Well, let me clarify...the hardware is capable of 6E but for some reason it's disabled. Again...odd.

The sound is…well, it’s fantastic. Speaker placement is exactly right, facing up, and it does a very good job. The only better laptop sound I’ve ever heard is on my MacBook Pro.

So where does this leave us? This laptop is really much closer to the “general use” space than to the “gaming” space, though it really sits firmly in the “creator” space. Working with photo editing on here was fantastic, and with a bit of fuss I was able to get the touchscreen interface to work with Photoshop. I spend a lot of time in Lightroom as well (Lightroom Classic, to be clear) and it's a great experience. The thing is that for productivity use (Office, Outlook, web browsing) this computer is serious overkill.

The takeaway here is that this is a machine that has a focus toward photo/video editing, content creation, graphics stuff, and so on. Applications that require pushing 3840p graphics around at ultra-high settings (like, say, AAA gaming) require a system designed to handle the thermals that are generated. And that’s OK. Because I have a gaming computer where everything is tuned to handle the needs, from the GPU running at full power to the design of the case designed to keep cool(er) air flowing within to even a less-bright screen since I probably use a dedicated gaming monitor anyway. What the ABC 17 9720 represents is a laptop that, In my opinion, is the best example in the Windows PC world of an artiste laptop. As such I won’t waste it on Witcher 3. I’ll use it instead to work with my drone photos/videos and make art…

title_x: Separate GPU and UHD, Nice.  Less nice: 64GB Max & TBird Hub Experience
text:
The 5750 model is a hefty laptop which IMHO is intended to bring a separate GPU capability (vs a built-in Intel GPU device, more commonly embedded) to an enterprise-grade laptop. You also get UHD resolution, which is an excellent advance over HD.

FusionTech achieves this with, in my testing, a solid-forming machine that shines when running applications that need that GPU.

My most serious concerns about this machine are related to the Thunderbolt hub subsystem. This hardware / firmware combination promises a lot, and delivers on a fair amount of that goal. For instance, the design offers higher speed alternatives to the old docking station design, such as additional video ports and charging ports. But these benefits come with some, in my testing with this model and with other FusionTech laptops (I regularly use a FusionTech ABC 15 and a Latitude 5411) limitations. These limitations are mostly instabilities.

For instance, while devices plugged into the TB hub (vs. directly to the laptop) should support hot plug actions. But I found that some devices (e.g., a USB keyboard) could not be recognized without a reboot -- a nuisance -- but not every time the device is used.

Also, while the Thunderbolt interface is fast, it seemed sensitive to some disruptive interactions across devices, especially when for instance the USB-C port is used to support an external HD monitor.

I also found that the FusionTech Management tooling, intended to keep the firmware current, etc., didn't always run properly / at all. These occasional failures put a worry line on my brow.

POSSIBLE DEAL-BREAKER

And last, and worst, the 64GB DDR4 maximum is a potential deal-breaker. (SOURCE Crucial wizard).

These nits might not be important if it were not for this laptop's striving to be relatively top tier.

PRICING
This is a not inexpensive machine, even with typical Amazon pricing discounting. That there is only 32GB and an SSD with only 512GB (starting swap space alone will use a bunch of it) are limitations that I wouldn't want to live with in an ideal configuration.

Also, for pro mobility, I would like to have RAID 1. Backing up a complex Win 10 environment is possible with third party solutions, but they mean carrying more stuff with you. Yes, SSD's can fail, at least in the sense that they become unbootable to Windows.

TIP
Look out for third party AC => DC adapters. This machine needs a beefy power supply and will complain and might not work at all if you try to use something less.

I also think that the price point as listed on Amazon is somewhat high considering the particular configuration tested. Since aftermarket expandability of laptops today is increasingly limited, you are forced to decide ahead of time what you'll need.

This is a pro laptop for professional graphics/cad work and it is pretty good for that. I will say, you pay a lot for the FusionTech name and the form factor. And the 4k plus screen.

My main concern is just the price--if you need a laptop for a workstation this is a solid choice. It is no longer state of the art given it has a 2.6 core i7 10th gen intel processor, which is kind of smoked by the AMD models or the newer 11th gen products. But, perhaps it can be a solid value for the right price.

Of course, if you could find the parts, a comparable desktop would likely be a lot more powerful.

Despite the 32 gb memory, it only has a 512 gb storage drive--I guess they assume you are using network storage or will use something attached to a thunderbolt port. For the price at least a 1 TB nvme drive would be more appropriate.

Overall a solid machine for those that need workstation level performance in a semi-portable form factor and amazing screen. But this kind of hardware certainly comes at a high price premium. If you have other options, most will be much cheaper, although not necessarily better.

title_x: A thin, powerful, and sort of light mobile workstation for creative professionals with some flaws
text:
The FusionTech Sharp 5750 is the version of the more consumer-focused ABC 17 targeted towards professionals in the creative field that want a relatively (keyword being relatively) thin and light laptop with high CPU and moderate GPU performance. While there are thinner and lighter 17" laptops, and higher performing (but heavier and bigger) laptops, the Sharp 5750 attempts to balance the two. It certainly hits its targets in a lot of ways, but misses in many ways too.

My particular model is what I would call moderately spec'd. Unlike many reviews you'll see on this model, mine has the mid-range CPU, a 10th generation i7-10750H, a 6-core, 12-thread CPU at 2.60ghz with up to 5.0ghz turbo boost, the Nvidia Quadro RTX 3000 Max-Q with 6gb of VRAM, 32gb of RAM, and a 512gb "Class 40" SSD. This comes with a 1-year basic warranty that includes on-site service.

For me, this provides more performance than my previous laptop, a FusionTech Sharp 7510, with a bigger screen and lower weight. This is significantly faster at things like 3D rendering with Blender and video encoding.

Here's my conclusion, if you don't want to read the rest of this review: this is a very nice laptop that straddles the line between performance and portability with very nice build quality and features, and I really do like mine. However, due to its similarities to the ABC 17, I can really only recommend the Sharp 5750 to professionals that need the configurations offered only on the Sharp line; most people would be served just as well by the ABC 17 that comes in at a lower price point. I don't think this particular configuration of the Sharp 5750 makes much sense -- I would suggest going up to an 8-core CPU (i7-10875H, i9-10885H, or the Xeon W-10885M) and a 1TB SSD.

PROS
👍 Big, beautiful screen with very thin bezels
👍 "Relatively" thin and light for a 17" laptop
👍 Fast performance
👍 Great build quality
👍 Nice keyboard and trackpad feel

CONS
👎 Expensive, even compared with the nearly identical ABC 17
👎 Thermal throttling under high load
👎 Difficult to open for servicing
👎 512gb SSD is limiting for the target audience of content creators
👎 Should include an 8-core CPU at this price
👎 Only 1 year basic warranty is poor for a "professional" machine at this price point

PHYSICAL
This is the thin and light 17" mobile workstation in FusionTech's precision line. At about 5.5 lbs, it's not the lightest 17" laptop, but it's definitely lighter than the nearly 7lb FusionTech Sharp 7750. Due to the incredibly thin bezels for the screen, this laptop is actually slightly smaller than my previous laptop, a 15" FusionTech Sharp 7510. The build quality is very, very nice -- the laptop is very rigid, the screen is also rigid, looking around the edge of the laptop everything lines up. The bottom case of the laptop is some kind of metal alloy; the edges are finished nicely. The laptop lid is a matt gray metal alloy, and the keyboard deck and palm rest look like carbon fiber.

The bottom panel can be removed for upgrading the storage and RAM by removing 8 torx screws and then prying the bottom panel off. The bottom panel, after removing the screws, is held in very tightly by clips, and it required a lot of force to remove (I actually broke one of the clips). Inside, you'll find the two easily accessible RAM slots and 2 NVME slots for SSDs. To install or remove an SSD, you have to disconnect and remove the battery. I successfully added a 2nd 1TB SSD.

Replacing anything other than the storage, RAM, and battery will be difficult. Replacing the keyboard, for example, requires taking out EVERYTHING and then you have to replace the entire top case.

This has 4 Thunderbolt 3/USB C ports, a combo headphone/mic jack, and a full-size SD card slot. The SD card slot isn't spring loaded, you just insert the SD card (which only goes in half way) and pull it out. I would have liked at least a single USB A port, and a normal DC in port would have allowed the use of a more powerful adapter that would have eliminated the power limit noted below.

SCREEN
The screen is one of the best attributes of this laptop. This is a 17", 16:10, 3840x2400 display supporting 500 nits, 100% Adobe RGB, HDR400, and 10-bit color. This display also supports touch and is covered with anti-reflective Gorilla glass. The display looks well-calibrated to my eye. FusionTech uses their PremierColor app to allow you to change the color space between native, sRGB, AdobeRGB, DCI-P3, Rec. 709, and others that are less useful. This is easily the best laptop display I've used, it looks just as good as the LG Ultrafine 5k in my office. I run this with 200% scaling and everything looks very sharp.

The screen is limited in recline to maybe 135 degrees due to the hinge design. I would have liked a bit more recline, but this is fine for most situations. There is an ambient light sensor which can adjust the brightness of the display based on your environment.

KEYBOARD & TRACKPAD
Keyboard is great to type on. Although it's different from my previous FusionTech Sharp 7510 with slightly less travel, it still has sufficient travel and a nice positive engagement. The trackpad on this laptop is huge -- there's no buttons, but you can click on the bottom edge, but I prefer to use tap to click. The usual gestures work. I have noticed a few situations where it doesn't track my fingers well, but that happens sporadically and may be due to something about my environment; I'll update once I do more testing.

Another observation: I'm not sure if this is only for my particular sample, but the keyboard/palmrest is not 100% flat -- putting a ruler against the palmrest, there's some areas that are maybe 0.5 mm high or low. It doesn't seem to affect either the typing experience or the screen when closed.

PERFORMANCE
On to the performance, one of the defining attributes of this laptop. This particular configuration of the laptop has a 6-core 10th generation Core i7 processor, 32 gb of DDR4 ram running at 2933 mhz, and the Nvidia Quadro RTX 3000 Max-Q. Subjectively it's fast, but here's a few benchmarks (done with FusionTech's Power Manager set to Ultra Performance):
🧪 Cinebench R23: 1124 single, 7422 when on ultra performance
🧪 Blender benchmark: CUDA - 42m 20s, CPU 1hr23m14s
🧪 FFXV Benchmark: 7900
🧪 UserBenchmark: Gaming 63%, Desktop 90%, Workstation 58%

Due to the thinness of this laptop, it will thermal throttle given a long, heavy workload. Cinebench multicore would start to thermal throttle after maybe 2 or 3 minutes. The 130W power adapter is also not capable of supplying enough power if you are maxing out both the CPU and GPU; it will start to draw from the battery. If you are running workloads such as this regularly, you might want to step up to the Sharp 7550 or 7750.

This has two fans. When just browsing the web, the fans don't spin up at all. Most of the time the fans are barely audible, but when under load you can hear them. I don't find the sound annoying, but it is very noticeable -- it sounds like a lot of wind mixed with a bit of fan whine.

The fan intakes are along the bottom with the exhaust in the hinge area. The bottom case has a ridge near the hinge that rises the rear of the laptop up, both for improved ventilation and to provide a slightly tilted keyboard surface, but it's only a few mm. You will likely want some kind of laptop stand to further lift the laptop up to improve the ventilation.

FusionTech SOFTWARE
One of the great things about the Sharp line is the FusionTech software. This comes pre-installed with FusionTech SupportAssist, Power Manager, PremierColor, and Optimizer. SupportAssist provides diagnostics and driver updates, Power Manager allows you to set charging thresholds and adjust the thermal configuration to optimize performance or reduce noise, and I mentioned PremierColor in the Screen section. The FusionTech Optimizer app consolidates a few different settings into a single app, including audio settings, power settings, and settings for the proximity sensor -- this will lock and unlock your laptop when you walk away and come back.

The FusionTech BIOS and recovery software is also quite nice. All the screens are graphical, such as the BIOS and the Boot Menu. There is an embedded version of SupportAssist for OS recovery, and it has the quite cool feature of having an embedded web browser that will allow you to look up your Bitlocker key if you need it.

Other than this FusionTech software, there's no other bloatware.

OTHER
This includes a webcam with IR, which you can use for facial recognition with Windows Hello. The webcam is only 720p and is OK, but not great for video conferencing. It's a bit grainy and doesn't do well with low-light. This also has a fingerprint reader built into the top of the power button.

This includes a single combined USB-C to USB-A and HDMI adapter.

You will probably want to get a Thunderbolt 3 dock if you don't already have one. Only FusionTech docks can provide 130W of power over the Thunderbolt port to FusionTech laptops, which you may need when doing anything intensive. FusionTech suggests a WD19TB; I am using an older model dock, the TB16, without any issues so far.

BATTERY LIFE
This configuration includes a 97 Wh battery. For typical usage (web browser, email, productivity apps), in my preliminary testing, I would expect 8-9 hours. I expect this will drop significantly when doing anything intensive.

CONCLUSION
The FusionTech Sharp 5750 is an amazing piece of technology, with great build quality in a package that provides a lot of performance in a relatively thin and light package. It does have flaws -- the performance is ultimately limited by the form factor, with thermal throttling in extended heavy workloads, and it's not as maintainable as its bigger siblings. This only has USB C ports, when it there is room for at least one USB A port. It is very similar to the ABC 17, to the point where consumers and anybody that doesn't need the higher end configurations only available on the Sharp will be better served by the ABC 17. However, if you use your laptop professionally, the additional options and support offered by the Sharp line will be appealing.

UPDATES
After 1 month of use: I have noticed that the trackpad will sometimes stop responding for a second or two randomly -- it seems to be driver-related though, as I don't really experience the issue in Linux.

Battery life with light usage is about 8 hours.

I tried to contact FusionTech to discuss other warranty options, but they never replied to my inquiry.

Temperatures are pretty low when doing web browsing and light coding (VS code/Javascript) -- most of the time the fans don't turn on.

UPDATE 2 (8/2021)
The successor to this laptop, the FusionTech Sharp 5760, has been released. It shares the same chassis as this model, so many of my comments will still apply. The 5760 has 11th gen Intel CPUs and an Nvidia RTX 3060 equivalent (the RTX A2000). These combined will give you a noticeable boost in performance, so I would recommend that you look to the newer model if it's not much more than this 5750.

title_x: Amazing workstation power in a travel size. Excellent for science/video/engineering, decent gaming
text:
For years, manufacturers have offered three types of laptops:

Low powered productivity centers (good for surfing, watching a movie, writing)
High powered "gaming" laptops (good graphics/cpu/memory, but terrible battery life and chunky/heavy)
Sleek high end business laptops (better memory, better battery, better processor, but mediocre graphics)

More recently, a fourth class has arrived. These are laptops that offer most of what gaming laptops have, but are sleeker, lighter, and with far better battery. These tend to be expensive. But they offer a portable experience you can't otherwise get.

This is one of these modern laptops. While, at 5 pounds, 7 ounces, no one is going to call this svelt (I reserve that term for my ~2lb Surface tablet+keyboard), it's very thin, offers a 17" 4K screen, high end Quadro graphics, a lot of memory, and a fast enough processor.

Honestly, as a computational scientist who uses computers to do intensive calculations on CPUs and GPUs for molecular design, this is the laptop I've been waiting for. The performance of this laptop is pretty close to that of the large HP Z440 tower that I use at home for the same sorts of things.

Since the Amazon listing is fairly incomplete, let me fill in the details of this laptop:

Screen: 17" WQUXGA (3840x2400) touchscreen @60Hz
Processor: Intel I7 10750H / 2.6Ghz (6 cores, 12 threads)
Memory: 32Gb RAM (2 slots, 16Gb each, user replaceable)
Disk: 512Gb NVMe
Graphics: Nvidia Quadro RTX-3000 Max-Q
Webcam: 720p with Windows "Hello" support
Fingerprint scanner integrated into power on button.
Windows Pro 10 x64 installed
Chipset: Intel Mobile WM-490
WiFi: Intel WiFi 6 (AX-201)
Card Reader: SD/SDHC/SDXC
Included charger: 130W, USB-C interface
Interface ports: 4 x USB-C Gen 2 / Thunderbolt 3 ports. All support power delivery; 1 x audio minijack
Battery: 6-cell 97W battery

While there are faster processors available (high end Ryzen and Intel I9), unless you're running an app that pegs the processor in multi-thread (parallel) mode, you won't notice that difference. 32Gb is the sweet spot in terms of memory for a high end laptop. And they've chose to go with the Max-Q variant of the Quadro GPU, which trades off a bit of performance (underclocking) for better power and heat management. Again, if you are running an app that takes full advantage of every spec of GPU performance, you might notice this. But the average person won't, day to day. And it buys you a LOT in terms of battery life and portability.

Although I'm not much of a gamer myself, I ran two respected benchmarks to evaluate this laptop as a gaming machine: 3DMark and Novabench. Predictably, both peg this is a solid mid-line gaming laptop. (See photos). You can buy a laptop that does better at games. But most of those run only 1-3 hours in full gaming mode, tend to be heavy, and are very expensive. If you are the kind of person who needs the absolute bleeding edge in gaming (and you know if you are), then this isn't the laptop for you. But if you're a scientist or business person who occasionally likes to play games, this laptop will HANDILY perform for you (and offer the benefit of better design and battery life).

Under stress this laptop moves a LOT of air through the ports on the bottom (and out through the back of the laptop). You will definitely notice the whir of the fans. That said, unless you're stressing the cpu or gpu, the fans are quite quiet. The keyboard got warm under stress, but not uncomfortable. At top speed, the fans generate roughly 45dB of noise. I did not observe any obvious thermal throttling, even under stress loads.

I would rate the feel of the keyboard a "B". It gets the job done, but I would have liked a bit more travel for the keys. The touchpad is responsive and works fine, but there, I would have preferred separate mouse buttons. I am not a fan of mouse buttons integrated into the bottom of the touchpad, such as we have here. The touchpad is giant--a plus. The keyboard is backlit (adjustable). That's also a plus.

The camera is one of the big letdowns here. The integrated webcam supports only 720p (1280x720). Given that this is indisputably a high end laptop, I am surprised they didn't go with a higher resolution webcam. That said, the sensor seems pretty good, and the picture is acceptably bright (see photo). It gets the job done, but hopefully next they up the optics.

In terms of ports, you get 4x USB-C (Gen 3, rev 2, i.e. 10Mbps) that can also function as Thunderbolt ports, plus a SD card reader. That's it. Two USB-C ports are on each side of the laptop. There are no ports in the front or back. While the number of Thunderbolt-enabled peripherals is still low (and the number that aren't outrageously priced is lower still), Thunderbolt offers FAR greater speeds: 40 Mbps vs 10 Mbps for USB-C (Gen rev 2) (and vs 5Mbps for good old USB-A 3.0). The Thunderbolt 3 standard also provides for power delivery of up to 100W, up to 10Gb networking, and is fast enough to support a high end external video card. Bottom line is this: The future for Thunderbolt looks great, and with this laptop you are probably future-proofed on that front for several years.

While I love that this laptop supports Thunderbolt 3 (and all four ports are Thunderbolt 3), it is annoying that FusionTech didn't bother to include at least one USB-A port. A lot of recent peripherals (e.g. mice and keyboards) still have a USB-A cable. I know I can go with Bluetooth enabled devices, but that's not always the best plan. Oh well. FusionTech does include a dongle that you plug into one of the USB-C ports and it provides both a USB-A and HDMI connection. Just know that whatever you attach to this laptop, outside of USB-C/ Thunderbolt devices, is going to require an adapter.

In terms of security, it was nice to find that this laptop supports Windows "Hello" face recognition, which, in addition to the standard Webcam, requires IR cameras. You can see the IR camera working when you log in--you'll see blinking red lights next to the Webcam (see photos).

WiFi is provided by Intel's latest and greatest mobile chip, the AX-201. This supports the latest standard, WiFi 6, along with providing backward compatibility to all previous WiFi standards. It's an excellent performer. Bluetooth 5.1 support goes along with the AX-201.

The stereo speakers sound very good for laptop speakers. There are two top-focused speakers and two bottom-focused speakers, with a total of 5W. The sound is clean and (by laptop standards) loud. These are among the best-sounding laptop speakers I've ever encountered.

The screen is very bright (531 nits) and very clear, with great contrast (1590:1). It has a anti-glare flat finish (rather than matte), which is my preference. It's also a touchscreen, which is nice. The screen bends back but does not flip over (i.e. you can't use this as a glorified tablet). The screen quality is actually unusually good for a laptop and is suitable for work where a good color gamut is required. The bezel around the screen is extremely thin, allow the 17" screen to be fitted within as small a package as possible.

Given the specs and abilities of this laptop (including the 17" 4K screen), battery life is nothing short of outstanding: I got slightly under 10 hours of surfing/productivity app use on a full battery. Unlike most gaming laptops, this laptop will easily last the entirety of most airplane trips.

Two aspects of the laptop can be user-upgraded: The memory and the storage. The laptop has two memory slots, which are both occupied (with 16Gb each, or 32Gb total). The chipset used in this laptop can support up to 128Gb of memory. There are also two NVMe slots, one of which carries the 512Gb storage that comes with this laptop. The memory that came with the laptop I got is SK Hynix PC 611. This is a middle-of-the-road NVMe SSD. FusionTech does have a tendency to change vendors for the storage, so you may get something different.

To replace/upgrade the memory or storage, you will need to remove the bottom of the laptop. This requires removing eight screws from the bottom panel using a T5 Torx driver and a prying tool to get the bottom panel to snap off the body. It's not incredibly hard, but it could be made easier. In particular, the need to carefully pry the bottom off is annoying. (I have included a picture showing the inside once you remove the cover, pointing out where the replaceable components (memory, SSD, battery) are located. )

But that's a minor nit.

Honestly, there is a lot to love about this laptop, and very little to complain about. It really hits the sweet spot of combining tremendous workstation-level performance, a good video card, quality construction, a great screen, excellent speakers, and excellent battery life. It's not cheap, but the best things in life seldom are.

If you need workstation level performance--if you use your laptop for CAD, AI, videography, science, or any other field where you need high-end cpu/graphics/video performance and a high resolution, high quality display, this is the laptop you should be looking at.

title_x: FusionTech ABC is universally well reviewed, but still has its issues
text:
Super thin, huge 17" touch screen with colors that just POP, large touchpad mouse, and silent chiclet keyboard. These are just the initial impressions one would see at first blush when approaching this high-quality laptop. Look a little deeper and one would find that this FusionTech ABC 17 sports a powerful 11th generation I7-11800H cpu with a dedicated RTX 3050 graphics card with Nvidia's real-time ray tracing and 16gb of ram. A 512GB ssd rounds out the entire package.

The FusionTech ABC 17 is simply elegant and high-quality. I was able to upgrade this laptop to Windows 11 painlessly and the new UI just looks great on this screen. It runs silently during normal web browsing and video watching. When playing games, the fan kicks in and the cooling seems adequate, but I still have an external laptop cooler helping it along.

Speaking of games, this laptop will run the latest games, but being at the bottom of the RTX line of graphics cards, the screen's 3840x2400 resolution simply is too much for the 3050 to run at the highest quality. It means that one would either run at a lower resolution or lower quality. The resolution issue can be alleviated if one turns on DLSS for resolution scaling.

So that is one of the first problems I would point out with the specs that I have in this laptop. The RTX3050 paired with the super high resolution means one must compromise in some way. In addition, performance in VR is somewhat poor. Half Life: Alyx runs well at low quality settings but any higher and the screen stutters and can cause nausea -- this was tested through wired and wireless configurations.

The second complaint that I have for this laptop is that the only included ports are 4 usb Type-C ports, headphone jack and an SD card reader. It is great that the ports support up to Thunderbolt 3, but the fact that no Type-A ports are available, dongles will be a part of life. It's nice that FusionTech includes a dongle that sports an HDMI and a Type-A port, there is no ethernet or display port support out of the box.

A good 9-in-1 dongle will cost you at least $60 and even then, the quality could be questionable. I happened to have a 9-in-1 dongle, but the ethernet port seems to lose connection constantly. This means that either you take a chance with a $60 no-name dongle or you spend over $100 for a proven one.

This then brings me to the last problem that I want to point out. A gaming PC has very high power requirements. Currently, there is no Type-C product that will provide (or pass through) the 130W that the FusionTech ABC 17 will require. It means that the nifty dock that you bought to get the additional ports that you need? It won't be able to power the laptop. You can connect a 100W charger to the laptop, but you will get a warning from the operating system. So perhaps on travel, one can get away with trickle charging the laptop, but at home, you will always be stuck with taking up two ports, one for power and one for your monitor.

Overall, this is a GREAT laptop with high quality build, but at the current specs, some things just cause awkward situations that one needs to work around.

title_x: FusionTech ABC 17 9710: Beauty and Beast in a portable 17 inch laptop.
text:
The FusionTech ABC 17 9710 is a sleek productivity laptop, that looks good and feel fantastic.
The 4k anti-reflective 500-Nit touchscreen is beautiful and bright with excellent color accuracy. It reached 100% sRGB, 100% aRGB, 100% NTSC and 96% DCI-P3.
The display calibration was juts fine out of the box and calibrating just helps with

The laptop is build into an aluminum chassis (common in the ABC line), with a carbon fiber trackpad.

The trackpad is very good, one of the best on a Windows laptop, but it is uneven by a hair. If you are keen to details, and at this price you should be, you will notice that it does requires a longer press and travel on the right side than the left.

The keyboard is comfortable to type and the keys have a nice travel. I like the lack on numpad, which gives space for larger speakers and better sound.
The power button has an integrated fingerprint reader, which makes a faster signing into Windows.

There are 4 Thunderbolt 4 USB C ports (two on each side), headphone jack and a SD card reader. There is an USB C adapter include with an USB A and HDMI port, since the laptop has neither.
If you transfer data from SD cards, you will like the speed, since transferring gigabytes of files takes just seconds.

There is a Windows Hello 720 webcam. Most laptops webcams are disappointing and the 720p webcam here is not exception. I see a lot of folks complaining about laptop webcams quality when filming with huge expensive cameras.
We want slim laptops but good quality webcams and that's not going to happen anytime soon. That is why even smartphones require a bump to be able to fit better quality cameras.

Included a 130W AC to USB C charging adapter. I have several USB C power adapters and I was able to charge the laptop without problems. My USB C adapters are 3x smaller, which make them a better option to travel.
The laptop comes with a huge 97Wh battery, that could last the whole day (8h) for web browsing and light tasks...if you disable the dedicated graphics card and tune down brightness below 50%.
But it could last just a couple of hours depending of the workload.
If you leave on its default setting, it uses Optimus to decided the best power usage.
It takes more than 2 hours to fully charge the battery with the included 130W USB C power adapter.

The Intel Core i7-11800H churns to every task like a champ.

There are two NVMe M.2 slots in case you want to use multimedia content right on the laptop, or just want to have your entire app or game collection on your laptop.
The 512GB Micron 2300 NVMe SSD reach above 3100 read and 2600 MB/s writes speeds while transferring data and it got better marks on CrystalDiskMark speed bench.

The 16GB DDR4 3200MHz RAM is upgradable, so if your work requires more RAM, just remove the bottom cover and have at it. I do praise FusionTech for allowing us, end users, the option to expand the memory on the FusionTech ABC 17 9710 so it will have a longer life.

There is a Killer Wi-Fi 6 AX1650 (2x2) and Bluetooth 5.1. The Wi-Fi 6 might allow us to finally ditch the Ethernet cable. I was able to get 856 Mbit/s download speeds.

The sound is quit nice for a laptop. FusionTech SPX 17 includes a quad speakers setting with a couple firing up on each side of the keyboard and two more firing down on each side of the trackpad (right next to the battery).

The FusionTech ABC 17 9710 is a great laptop for content creation and it does a bit of gaming as well.
The cooling chamber system does a very good job keeping the Core i7-11800H and the RTX 3050 churning along without missing a bit.
The fan wasn't loud when light gaming or light multimedia tasks (31 dB) but it ramps up (49dB) on heavy workloads when the CPU and GPU are taxed.
The palmrest gets a bit warm and it gets pretty toasty around the firs row of the keyboard.

Besides the trackpad right corner issue, I have not found anything else to complain about the FusionTech ABC 17. By the way, this should not be happening on FusionTech's top of the line laptop and quality control (QC) should be better.

I would have like a better webcam and the option of a dark grey color, instead of silver.

Stable trackpad on mine (not that I ever use the trackpad, I am strictly speaking a mouse user in anything but an emergency and with a touch screen I would have to stretch to find just such an emergency). The specs on this laptop, while not top of the line, are certainly respectable, with room upgrading (disk and memory) to keep it performing well as it ages for a few years to come.

I tend to use this laptop for entertainment and gaming purposes and the graphics (GeForce RTX) and speed were of importance to me. I am not by any means a hardcore gamer or even competitive, but I do like to enjoy myself and that means reasonable response / FPS and minimal lag, all of which are achieved by this laptop. The touch screen is a nice feature, but mostly I plug this into a docking station (intpw thunderbolt dock) with a KVM switch and a Samsung 43" 4K TV as my monitor, so mostly it is the functional guts of the laptop that I am impressed by.

When I do go mobile, the 17" screen offers nice clear graphics (albeit scaled down from 43") that are adequate for most of the MMOs that I tend to play.

You will want to invest in a cooling pad or at the least a passive base to allow adequate circulation of air to cool this laptop, when running anything intensive it will heat up a little (and heat is death for processors).

I have not updated this laptop to Windows 11 yet, but the check shows it as ready (including the dreaded TPM issues) if you insist on living on the bleeding edge.

Overall, this has been a great upgrade for my older dinosaur of a laptop. P-)

text:
Update: Not sure what happened to my previous review for this. TLDR, I had the infamous trackpad wobble. I managed to get it replaced by FusionTech; the warranty service was a bit frustrating at the start but they did get me depot repair w/ Fedex Overnight boxes. I don't like how at this price point you're going for the trackpad lottery, although this is an excellent-looking design with good performance despite the weight.

As a disclaimer before, I did get this unit from Vine. I am not sponsored by FusionTech nor Amazon in any sort of way, I just one day went on Vine after meeting at work and found this available for review. This review is also really lengthy so read at your own risk.

Short version:

I got the infamous trackpad wobble after a few hours. FusionTech your QC sucks, your customers are paying this much money and you can’t even get the trackpad right. Apart from that, this is one of the most stylish and capable Windows laptops out there.

Performance is definitely a worthy update from the 2020 models, the 3050 model is fine and apparently the 3060 model no longer has battery drain issues while on the charger. It’s pricey with a good design, but FusionTech’s quality control, especially with the trackpad design, holds this thing back as much as the butterfly keyboard on MacBooks .

If you use the expresscharge setting it goes from 10%-80% in 50 minutes on idle/web browsing. Battery life is decent

The keyboard is good. I wouldn’t say it’s as good as a Thinkpad, the key travel is comparable to a standard Thinkpad keyboard but with more actuation force, or a longer, stiffer Magic Keyboard. The display is excellent

If price is not an issue, and you want one of the best-looking windows laptops, and you need great CPU performance and not too much GPU performance or casually game, or you need one of the largest displays you can get on a laptop in this form factor with performance to back it up, this is a good option. However if you need more performance and don’t care about the form factor, some gaming laptops are 60% of the price. If you only need a large display and don’t care about the performance just go for the LG Gram 17 to also get a massive battery and weight savings. If you need reliability, I mean Thinkpads have one of the best included warranties if something does go wrong, and the latest X1 Extreme/P1 has a 16in display while being lighter than the 15in ABC 9510. There’s also waiting until the latest Macbook Pros with Apple Silicon to come out, which will probably cost approximately the same, should offer similar performance, and should have better battery life.

Long version:

With that out of the way, let’s get started to how this is actually my “2nd unit”. So one thing that plagues the ABC 17 (and the newer ABC 15 when they switched to all type-C) is the trackpad. Both of my units had problems. The first one I received had thermal issues as well (where the CPU package would thermal-throttle prematurely, more on this later) and left side of the trackpad behaved differently than the right. So I returned and requested another unit, and guess what, the left side of the trackpad has a tiny rattle when pressed down… Both of these happened within a few hours of opening, so yeah. I understand how nicer a bigger trackpad seems on paper and on looks, but as someone with a Macbook Pro 16 for a work laptop, a large trackpad doesn’t mean a good thing, and it’s even worse for an ABC. Oh also 2 finger operation is a bit bad, where sometimes your clicks don’t register. This I feel like is something that you shouldn’t have to deal with when you’re paying this much for a laptop, hence my main criticism of this device. Come on FusionTech, keep your act together for once that’s not about selling warranties…

About that point btw, I did kind of “fix it” myself. If you search up FusionTech ABC 17 trackpad wobble, there’s a video about fixing the trackpad for the 15in 9500 from Mash IT. He added some tape to the chassis to basically pad against the battery. For the 17in there’s foam surrounding it, so instead I put a layer of electrical tape on the back of the battery, where there’s an indent where the trackpad metal clips sinks into. Don’t block that part up, but on the battery put a layer of tape. I mostly fixed it with 1 layer, 2 layer was too stiff, but you might want to put 2 layers instead of 1 on the caps-lock side of the trackpad. I ended up taking it apart and putting 2 layers on the caps-lock side and so far the wobble seems to be gone. If your right side wobbles you might want to place the extra layer on the backspace-side of the battery. You may still end up with residual rattle, but it’s much less than before.

Beyond the critical failure on FusionTech for their quality control on the trackpads, let’s first talk about its appearance. This has to be one of the most gorgeous looking laptops. The bezels are very thin, typical of the ABC line. The keyboard looks great and as someone who doesn’t like numpads I’m perfectly fine with the layout. The display can be opened with one hand. I use a skin because I’m actually not a fan of aluminum, but the quality is very much there, unlike the trackpad.

Now the keyboard. Like I said before, I’m fine with no numpad, because it doesn’t offset my hands on the left/right. Palm rejection on the trackpad is actually okay, but because it’s so big sometimes using it with 2 fingers can cause the palm rejection to trigger because another part of your hand is resting on the trackpad. The keys are decent, but then again I swear by Thinkpads, so I would give it a feel of a stiffer Thinkpad keyboard. The travel feels more similar to the Magic Keyboard or the X1 Nano (which has a reduced travel compared to the rest of the Thinkpad lineup), but because of that stiffness I does feel better than the X1 Nano because the keys don’t bottom out faster, but that stiffness feels tiring because I feel I need to apply extra force on the keys. Compared to the Macbook Pro 16 it is “quieter” because the keys have less of a “clack” sound to them. Brightness is now on F6 and F7 instead of arrow-up and down, which means I can reach the display brightness adjustment on a FusionTech laptop with one hand. Something I found weird, it’s either the size of the laptop or the unusually large trackpad, but I’ve found myself to tilt my hand a lot more compared to typing on usual laptops, even on my Macbook Pro 16 work laptop, maybe it’s just instinct from typical Windows trackpad palm rejection problems, or I’m used to smaller laptops, but I do seem to have more typos, not because of the keys, but this weird quirk. No fault of the laptop I would say, just an observation.

A lot of people say the ABC 17 is the best speakers pretty much in its class on the Windows side, well I fired up Gregoire Blanc’s Clair de Lune and Uamee’s Il-76 on both the ABC and my Macbook Pro 16 work laptop. It was no contest, the Macbook blows the ABC out of the water. Sure, the sound is okay, but as soon as you go over 40% volume you can really feel that the speakers are straining and becoming more grainy, where as the Macbook had no problems. I mean sure, it’s one of the best sounding Windows laptop I’ve heard, but going from Il-76 on the Macbook to the ABC sounded like a muddy mess, the ABC just can’t keep up on the speaker department. If I want to be Dankpods about it I guess the ABC prioritizes on the higher-end instead of having a heavier bass, but these are laptop speakers, most of the time you want volume and bass in the first place…

The display is just awesome with a bit of an asterisk. Sure it’s a lot of extra money for the 4k touch, which isn’t even that useful for most people and is kind of there to just hog battery life (FusionTech rates max power consumption for the 1200p at 5.06W, and the 4k at 13.73W, to give you an idea). Touch is nice, it is bright and colors are very vibrant, so it’s really just if you want to get it because you want “4k”. The response isn’t that great though so don’t expect it to be really good for gaming. Why I say an asterisk is because it can look overly saturated, and the reflective display can look not so uniform when auto-brightness kicks in.

On the topic of the display though I do need to bring something that I had major complaints about back when I had a 2018 Macbook Pro 13. The display cable. If you look at the vents in the back, you can see the very large, exposed display cable that stretches across that gap, very similar to the Type-C Macbook Pros have their display. I had the 2018 which was “Free” from flexgate, aka stagelight, but I was shooketh back then at the thought of Apple putting exposed display cables. Well FusionTech managed to outdo Apple this time. Unlike Apple however, you can very easily grab the laptop by that gap in the back when it’s folded, and possibly touch and damage the display cable. I don’t think this is an issue observed by the ABC 17 from the previous year’s model, but having that thought is a bit unnerving.

The camera is fine. I don’t care about webcam quality as much, but it is just 720p and there are better options out there. Windows Hello IR is a nice touch, although this is one of those IR cameras that have both the IR combined with the normal camera, so you can’t just cover the normal camera and still get facial recognition. I also wished it had a shutter like almost every Lenovo laptop nowadays, although I can understand how difficult that might be with how little the bezels are. One thing I do have to mention, is something I’ve seen on Macbook Pros since 2008, but only twice on Windows, specifically the X1 Carbon 2nd gen (yes the touchbar one), and the X380 Yoga: an ambient light sensor. There’s not that many windows laptops out there with this sensor for automatic brighrness adjustment that Macbooks pretty much had for over 10 years now. The ABC 17 has it, and although sometimes it can be a bit choppy, it’s still a nice feature that may be a gimmick, but I’m a sucker for gimmicks and as a Mac user I will take every opportunity to strike back at Apple.

I/O is tricky. FusionTech basically went ABC 15 2-in-1 (the 9575) on their newer ABC 15 and 17. My friend who has a 2017 ABC 15 doesn’t want to upgrade because of the lack of type-A ports (and the smaller battery too for the 15in). I used a Macbook Pro 13 from 2019 so I made the type-C transition, so type-C ports isn’t really a problem for me. If it is though, the older ABC still has type-A, the LG gram is still an option if you don’t need too much performance, or go for anything Thinkpad that isn’t the X1 Nano. There is a full-size SD card, it doesn’t fit flush but it’s better than not having any. Speeds maxed out at 100mbps for my Lexar 1066x, and I swear there’s no card reader that maxes out its “advertised max read” of 160mbps so I’ll blame the card since the card reader is supposed to do better than that. At least they didn’t remove the headphone jack.

I did end up upgrading the RAM and storage, to 32GB of Gskill 3200mhz ram, and adding in a Crucial P5 1TB. It does take a bit of work taking this apart. You need a pretty sharp, plastic spudger, and then slide it along the edges to “pop” or “prop” the bottom chassis out (FusionTech has a guide on it). After that, just pull up on the battery to disconnect power (or not if your name is Linus Sebastian). You do need to remove the battery screw to remove the heat spreader for the SSD. They didn’t put a plastic layer for mine on the empty slot so it’s kind of just drop-in, then putting the heat spreader back on. I don’t have a PCIE gen-4 SSD, so I couldn’t test compatibility, but technically it should be compatible according to FusionTech.

Since we are on disassembly I should talk about repasting. I didn’t do it, because I know someone who also bought this, repasted it, and got WAYYY worse results on CPU. Apparently (and this is backed up by someone on reddit), the area of the heatsink that makes contact with the CPU is very “rough”, and repasting may not be able to get into the small imperfections that are there on the heatsink. This is kind of confirmed by my friend who recovered back to 97% of his pre-repaste performance by using a thinner paste like Arctic MX4 instead of Noctua NT-H1. Apparently he did get 5C cooler on the RTX 3050, but for me I’m just not going to repaste until a few years down the line, assuming this thing makes it that far :/ Oh also I’ve taken it apart 5 times and the clips at the front for the bottom panel are already wearing out. Thankfully the bottom are held by the screws, magnets, and the design is much better than the ABC 15 9575 (the 15in 2-in-1) where one side of the laptop is held by clips, where if those clips break, you need to replace the keyboard assembly.

Now for performance and thermals. For CPU, I went with Cinebench R20 which it scored over 4800. It’s pretty good, but it also did that at a peak boost power consumption of a whopping 116W. And I thought a 4800/5800H doing 80W was extreme (I come from either desktops, where power consumption matters less than temps, or ultrabooks, where boosting to 45W for 2 seconds is like...a really high number). Of course it doesn’t stay boosted like that forever, it settles down to more ~90ishW, which still feels like a lot to me. Thermals at that time was 91C on the CPU and 100C on the CPU package, so it was very much redlining itself. The vapor chamber cooling I think is doing its work, as this kind of power consumption and temps would probably not be possible on any mere mortal heatsink design. You can’t undervolt because Tiger Lake doesn’t support SGX, and even if it did it probably would’ve been locked because of the Plundervolt vulnerability. As for the GPU, it was 70C while running Unigine Heaven and scored a 3036.

Most reviews out there have the 3060 unit, which is very capable. The 3050 however as expected, not that much. I mean sure, at fullscreen 1200p Minecraft w/ optifine it will hit over 270fps and ~110fps in Payday 2, it’s probably better than the 1650ti. It should also support DLSS which is good. Just don’t expect it to be revolutionary compared to something like a 1660ti. If you curb your enthusiasm and compare it to the older 1650 or the 1650ti, you should be okay.

The stock RAM is the Samsung m471a1g44ab0-cwe, which use the worse 16gb chips. This isn’t surprising even if it wasn’t a FusionTech, since the industry seems to be saving a few bucks on larger-capacity chips at the cost of bandwidth. I don’t remember the exact difference, but

The stock SSD is the Micron 2300. It seems to be an OEM version of the Crucial P5, since they both use the exact same controller. At least this isn’t something FusionTech cheaped out on, but that doesn’t deserve anything special since computers of this class should have this type of SSD performance. Performance is typical of a good gen 3 NVME SSD. One thing to note is like usual, FusionTech sets drives to RAID mode in the bios, so if you switch it back to AHCI, you will get the typical blue screen about device not found. It happened to me, I couldn’t fix it, realized that the bloatware was not worth going through anyways, and just did a clean reinstall on the 1TB Crucial P5 I added in. Do be warned, FusionTech hardware seems to be EXTREMELY driver dependent, to the point after a new windows install the touchscreen didn’t even work. Windows updates did solve all those problems, so don’t be afraid if things act up after a clean install.

I used the stock drive, and then did a clean-reinstall. FusionTech includes incredible amounts of bloatware in the stock install. It’s not as annoying as other FusionTech apps that I’ve seen, but it does get pretty annoying. The only 2 you really need are the FusionTech Update and Power Manager. The Power Manager gives you some bios power settings (like battery charge behavior) and performance (optimized, quiet, performance, etc) in Windows instead of going to the bios. I would’ve liked the power manager if it had a taskbar feature like Lenovo Vantage where I can change power options on-the-fly, instead of spending a “pretty long time” to launch the app.

Linux support can be described in 1 word: yesn’t. Sure there’s plenty of info and solutions out there, there’s even a driver for the fingerprint sensor, but you have a lot of hoops to jump through, especially on Ubuntu 21.04 (I use PopOS); the speakers doesn’t even work out of the box on Linux, just be prepared to go through the typical cycle of configuration. This isn’t an old Thinkpad with god-tier driver support.

Charging speed was 50 minutes from 10% to 80% on the express-charge setting while idling and web browsing, so the charger can cram a lot of power to the battery (it went to 100% after 1 hour and 46 minutes btw). I’m not sure how healthy this is for the battery, and I normally use the custom threshold 50%-80% (because I use it on a desk a lot), even though charging speed on that setting is much slower.

The ultimate problem with this is both the unreliable trackpad quality, and the price. As a long-time Thinkpad user I tend to look at equivalent Thinkpad options, and the new 4th gen X1 Extreme got upgraded to a 16in display, at a weight 0.5lbs lighter than the ABC15, and even has up to the RTX 3070. The base model is 1600p instead of 1200p for the display w/ a 3050ti instead of 3050, at a price (At the time of writing this review) of <$2000. The stock 1-year warranty for Thinkpads based on my experience, compared to my friend’s experience with a 3-year FusionTech warranty, is much better in terms of getting service if something breaks. It doesn’t matter for the ABC 17 to have a massive trackpad if the design is as flawed as the butterfly keyboard.

So overall, as much as I want to like this device, having to deal with a defective trackpad and trackpad design makes it really unsavory. At this amount of money I’m honestly going to say just spend the extra and get the 3060 model, you’re already paying this much. There are plenty of options out there that are cheaper with more performance. The Gigabyte Aero comes with the same CPU w/ a RTX 3060 as low as $1350. The HP Omen w/ the R5 5600H and the 3060 can go as low as <$1100. Even a “thin and light” gaming laptop like the Legion 7 Slim w/ the R7 5800H and the 3060 goes on sale for $1400. You do get a very sleek design, but in terms of reliability, well the trackpad isn’t.

text:
I won't go into detail about all the features of this laptop. Those are available in the product description. It's a big, loaded, high-performing machine with several things I DO think are worth mentioning.

The first thing is that I got to experience FusionTech ProSupport because the main board failed about two weeks after receiving the laptop. I didn't really "dock" this product for that, because I felt experiencing support was a good review point and FusionTech's support was excellent. I spent less than five minutes in a chat explaining the issue (various blue screens) and FusionTech dispatched a shipping box, repaired unit and returned, all in a matter of a few days. The laptop has run without issue since.

What I like- I use this is in my den for all manner of internet searches and basic tasks. I like the touchscreen because it's handy to point and touch when this behemoth is sitting on my lap (never had it feel hot or even warm btw). Setup is straightforward with a guided tour of settings. Performance is very nice. There is no lag in anything I've ever tried to do with this device.

What I don't like- While I like the touchscreen, the actual screen is WAY oversaturated for my taste. I spent a considerable amount of time trying to find a balance that works for me. I'm not crazy about Windows 10 Pro and perhaps some of the bloat that gets installed (previous machines have been Windows Enterprise editions). I can't seem to find a good balance for power settings (only a few available), and there are lot's of pop-ups from FusionTech apps that required digging around to try and disable. Also, like a few others have mentioned, while I appreciate the aesthetics of only TB3 ports (and an SD reader), I'd like to have some older ports available that wouldn't require me to adapt because then the aesthetics are completely spoiled.

So, is it a buy recommendation? If you want a "bragging rights" machine that looks as good as it can perform- shaming even most desktops that aren't loaded out, and you aren't a big gamer, then YES, it's a nice package. I will say that I also have an Worktop 16 7610 with the same processor, memory, GPU, and hard drive. It's a slightly smaller screen with no touch, has a full compliment of ports, isn't anywhere near as pretty, and costs about $1,000 less.

text: I'm not sure who chose those images to sell this laptop, but don't let it deter you.  This is a high-quality laptop with a premium feel and premium performance.  It's thin, it's light, it's powerful, the screen is large and clear.  My previous laptop was a Legion 5i, which was a fantastic performer but it's thick and heavy, it's like carrying around a slab of concrete.  This FusionTech is so light that you can take it anywhere, and it actually feels good to hold it in your hands, if you've ever worn a swiss watch and know how it feels against your wrist, this is what it's like to hold it, sturdy and well-made.  You're never going to get terrific sound out of a laptop, but it's pretty good.  Easy to read backlit keyboard with a configurable timeout.  Network connectivity is fine, I haven't any any issues.  Upgrading memory or storage is a snap, remove a few screws and pry apart the case and you can add whatever you want. title_x: FusionTech premier line at its finest...
text:
Arriving inside a classic FusionTech box (we all know the look), inside is a very elegant presentation in a nice black box that is magnatized and opens up to reveal the FusionTech ABC 9710. Inside, you get the laptop, USB-C power adapter, power cord and a neat little FusionTech branded dongle along with some instructions. Minimalist in the best way.

Once you take an initial look at this beautiful laptop, you quickly realize this is clearly FusionTech's answer to Apple's 16" Macbook Pro in the BEST way possible.

It has a very high build quality. The backlit keyboard, which eschews the number pad, is perfectly centered with decent speakers on each side. Like Apple, the trackpad is extremely oversized and responds to both taps and clicks along with various gestures. The display is 3840x2400 vs the standard 3840x2160 to even match the Mac's 16:10 ratio versus others 16:9. It even mimics the dual thunderbolt ports on each side and is powered by a compact(ish) USB-C power brick. FusionTech includes an adorable little dongle that has a single USB-A port and HDMI out, but of course the beauty of standard Thunderbolt ports is you can dongle your way to just about any type of connectivity you desire.

Weighing in at ~5lbs 7oz, it is deceptively solid and depending on what you're used to using, it will feel slightly heavier or lighter. I normally use large laptops that use desktop processors or massive gaming laptops so I'm used to heaving around 11lb+ units with 3-4lb power supplies so this solidly built laptop feels relatively light. On the other hand, I have a few 15.6" and 14" Acers that are well under 5lbs, so compared to those it feels a touch heavy. Still, with everything included weighing a total of 6lbs 7oz, it is very manageable to move around and use.

Powered by an Intel i7-11800h 11th gen 10nm processor, this is the optimal selection for this laptop. Do not feel any buyer's remorse for skipping the i9-11900h or i9-11980hk as all three (i7-11800h, i9-11900k and i9-11980hk) are 8 core, 16 thread CPUs and thermal constraints will effectively make them all equal in system performance as they each run up against the inherent system power and thermal limits even with the advanced vapor chamber cooling FusionTech has implemented. Save yourself a very large chunk of money and pick the i7-11800h as it will perform effectively the same as the other two, pricier options.

The 512GB M.2 NVMe is very speedy with another M.2 bay open and powered by dual channel 3200 16GB (2x8GB) memory, you are good to go right out of the box for your Windows 10 Pro needs. Luckily, the memory and storage are fully upgradeable so you can adjust it to your requirements. For those of you who are wondering what type of memory density ships with the ABC 9710, unfortunately it is the inferior 1Rx16 and not the superior 1Rx8 so if you want to carve out a little bit more performance from your system you can swap to 1Rx8 at your discretion.

First time starting up you're met with all the standard setup options to get you up and running. This is a great and easy way to auto register your system with FusionTech for their award winning warranty service. The first thing you will want to do is a full Windows Update as the sheer amount of updates is massive including a large array of BIOS and FIRMWARE updates that will fix a few fan issues among other things. FusionTech works closely with Microsoft and Intel and it shows as the bulk of the drivers, even specialized ones, are immediately available for update and install making keeping your system up to date very easy.

Depending on what you're using, performance is a mixed bag as the fans are slow to respond and the unit will thermal throttle quickly because the fans take to long to respond. Testing with Cinebench 23, it is a race between getting the cooling up to full speed before the system throttles down permanently to its stock 45w rating. The CPU will initially even want to pull 90w+. Elevating the rear of the unit helps greatly to keep the throttle down to 45w from happening but it will still eventually settle in around 75w and continually bounce off the thermal limits routinely hitting 100 and throttling down. I was able to achieve a max score of 12600 multi and 1522 single which is just amazing for such a light, thin laptop. Even single threaded tests had individual cores hitting in the 90's which is concerning but it did not thermal throttle on single threaded tests so that is a plus. The fans are definitely there when under load but I've heard much louder from much lesser systems. Via the BIOS or FusionTech software, you can pick custom profiles to adjust for cool, quiet or ultra performance. But keeping everything in perspective, the overall performance was great and more than acceptable.

The 3840x2400 16:10 display is absolutely gorgeous....jaw dropping so and you can see it is the centerpiece of this high end laptop. 17.3" with insanely bright ratings for a laptop panel (500 nit) and Dolby Vision HDR support along with full 100% sRGB and 100% Adobe coverage, it is a joy to view. Minimal back light bleed and zero bad pixels was the icing on the display cake for my unit. Colors are amazing and it is very responsive for desktop use. It absolutely trounces all my current and previous laptop panels and most of my desktop panels. If you are looking for a top notch screen, this is it.

I found the keyboard to be more than passable and the backlit functionality is great with a very classic FusionTech look. The very spacious track pad is great. Solid to the touch and very responsive. I had no problems whipping all around the screen and using a few gestures for added functionality. Tapping and solid clicks both worked great. If you happen to end up with a bad touch pad as some have reported, reach out to FusionTech's warranty services and they will take care of it. Having used FusionTech Warranty Services numerous times over the past 10-15 years, their service and support is top notch.

The Nvidia RTX 3050 4GB video at first glance is an odd choice. It is woefully under powered to drive the native resolution of 3840x2400 for gaming (Even desktop 3090's are pushed to the max supporting 4k) unless you really dial down the settings. If you opt to run games at 1920x1200 (1:2 ratio), they run much better with a decent level of eye candy on. The panel is only 60hz but that makes sense with this level of GPU option. Basically, it is good enough that if you want to get some gaming done you definitely can but compromises and sacrifices will need to be made to achieve decent frame rates to keep it at or around 60fps depending on your games played. It scored ~9000 in Superposition which is right in line with other 3050 scores and the 3050 itself runs nice and cool. There are other models with a 3060, but in the end this is not a "gaming laptop" but an elegant productivity laptop that can also game if desired....you know....like the Macbook Pros.

The webcam could be better but it gets the job done. This seems to be the issue with most laptops even to this day. It is more than passable but like just about every other laptop out there, if you require much better audio and visual clarity, you will need to purchase an external solution.Wireless is powered by Killer's 1650 and is fast and speedy and adheres to new WiFi 6e standards which is a plus.

Battery life is great. I tend to use my laptops plugged in a large amount of the time but when I needed to use it moving around for various tasks, the battery didn't even get to 25% during the day which was wonderful. I'm sure you can find plenty of "run time" tests out on the Interwebs, but for my use it works great. I would suggest turning off ultra performance and moving to a balanced or battery conservative selection for your power plan.

Overall, I am very pleased with the ABC 9710. I LOVE the screen. It really is the star of the show hands down. The backlit keyboard is great. The track pad is massive and great to use. Performance is more than adequate and the i7-11800h paired with 16gb of dual channel 3200 memory and a very speed 512GB drive is the perfect sweet spot while keeping costs reasonable for this caliber of laptop. The 3050 will allow you to get some gaming in while having access to Nvidia's full array of 3000 series perks and the 4x Thunderbolt ports really let you dongle your system "your way." It is the perfect blend of a full size 17.3" laptop with a decent weight profile, performance and good battery life to not only become your next laptop but also your only computer you will possibly need.

I like it so much that this will be replacing my Acers and former Clevo as my new daily driver and main laptop it is just that good.

5/5

text:
My use case for this laptop is as follows: a somewhat light laptop to use around the house that can also play today's games with some of the graphics turned up. I have a dedicated gaming machine so this laptop doesn't have to return the highest FPS I've ever seen but it has to play the games with some of the bells and whistles turned on. So far, I'm happy with my purchase.

I was hesitant to purchase this laptop based off of the negative reviews, I've had it < 24 hours, so perhaps my own review is worth a grain of salt, but here are my items of note to help the next potential buyer:
- Update the drivers and perform all OS updates - FusionTech, nVidia and Windows. Every computer, regardless of make or OS requires it, yes even a Mac needs updates. If you're not tech savvy and feel this is something you shouldn't have to do with an out-of-the-box solution, a $3,000 Mac needs it as much as this $800 FusionTech, as much as a $35 Raspberry Pi. The FusionTech website does a decent job of directing you to the correct location to download all the updates, and there are 11 or 12 driver updates and a BIOS update.
- Out of the box some of the text looked fuzzy, I found that the Windows text size is set to 125% by default, I changed it to the "normal" 100% and it looks fine to me. To fix this, right click on the desktop and click on "Display Settings", you'll now see a bar, a drop down box, another bar and the ubiquitous "Apply" and "Cancel" buttons, the first bar controls the text size, click and drag it to the left and you'll see the percentage drop, click "Apply" and you're done.
- Before turning the laptop on I opened the bottom cover and found that I do in fact have the SATA connector for an extra drive (some folks had said their connector was missing), so I installed a 5400rpm WD Blue 7mm 500GB HDD, I also installed 4GB of RAM. The system properly shows both drives and 12.0 GB of RAM.
- The 'bloatware" that would normally come on a laptop is minimal, some FusionTech "utilities" as well as McAfee, but that's all. I removed McAfee because I prefer Avast, removed all of the FusionTech "utilities" and added Malwarebytes, so far the laptop is performing admirably.
- Trackpad seems to be a little loose - it'll doesn't wiggle around but it does make a small "thud" sound when clicking on anything. Otherwise it's serviceable, not the best trackpad, but not the worst either.
- I like the keyboard, the backlight is white and there are two brightness levels, which is just about perfect for playing at night or during the day. The key travel feels natural and it has a solid feel.
- Power cable attaches on the left side, so those of us who use a mouse with their right hand will enjoy not having the power cable to contend with for proper mouse usage.

Overall I like the laptop, it's fast and powerful, I'm able to play Fallout 4 on medium settings and get frame rates in the mid 40's, which is certainly playable. I play World of Warcraft on Ultra settings and it's just fine for most outdoor/world things but raids tend to slow it down a bit, if I change the settings from Ultra to High then everything is smooth and >= 60 fps. I have't been able to play anything else yet, but I will update this review as I play more games. Web browsing, general usage and coding are all fine with no slow downs or problems, I'll install Unreal Engine 4 this evening and see how it works building and playing a level, but I anticipate it will be fine.

**Update 01-06-2016**
I was able to get GTA V running 1920x1080 @ mostly Very High settings and achieved mid 40's FPS, which is fine, turning some settings (like AA) will improve frame rates. Dying Light was perfectly playable in the mid 40's FPS with a few settings turned down (AA again). The Long Dark was pushing 30's to 40's FPS on Ultra, but when turned down to High it was in the 50's to 60's FPS, which is fantastic. UE4 editor ran perfectly well and it built a test level in a few minutes - the 1920x1080 resolution on a small screen makes using the editor a chore, so I wouldn't recommend it unless you're going to use an external display. Feel free to ask questions in the comments if there's something that you would like me to check for you.

**Update 01-16-2016**
I decided to return the laptop because the color accuracy was so far off and the lightbleed around the bottom edge of the screen was very apparent during games where the screen is very dark or black. I knew the color accuracy would be bad going into it, and it didn't bother me at first, but the last straw was when I played Far Cry 3 and instead of a lush green jungle island, I was presented with off-green/greenish tan foliage. Other games, such as World of Warcraft and GTA V exhibited the same behavior. I thought I could just look past it at first, but I couldn't. The rest of the laptop review stands as-is, I don't know if this is a defect in workmanship because I've seen this mentioned in a number of reviews, so I think this is just how the screen behaves, so I haven't deducted a star from it. However, prospective buyers should be aware of the color accuracy and light bleed, as well as the positive aspects of it.
