title_x: Great all around performer, absolutely beautiful screen
text:
EDIT: In regard to gaming and battery....I played an hour and a half of Untitled Goose Game without the laptop plugged in and then the battery died. For a low graphics game, I'm a bit surprised.

This is a good, balanced, ‘can do a bit of everything’ general use laptop. I know others will go into all the specs and details and what those mean, so I’m going to try and review this for the average person who doesn’t know what all that means.

It’s got a nice look to it. It’s slim, easy to carry, and will fit into any backpack or college class. It looks like a high end machine. Probably the first thing you’re going to notice when you power this up is how great the screen is. It has a 4K UHD display on an OLED screen with FusionTech’s Infinity Edge. It’s just beautiful. What you want to know from that is that things will look as nice on this screen as they do on your big expensive TV screen. Blacks are dark black, colors are vivid when they ought to be, and soft when they ought to be. The screen goes to the edge of the laptop, and the images nearly to the edge of the screen – there’s a tiny black frame around the edges, but I didn’t notice it…I actually had to boot it up and go look to see if there was any edge at all. Great for watching videos or streaming an online class.

The power cord has a tiny light on the plug where it goes into the laptop. While just a small thing, I find that it’s very useful, especially when travelling, to indicate that I’m actually plugged into a working outlet and not just wasting time hoping it’s charging when it isn’t. FusionTech put some attention to detail in this. The power cord is a bit over 9 feet long overall. The power brick is 3 feet from the wall plug end. The brick is nice and small; about twice the thickness of a smart phone and similarly sized. Photo is of an LG V30 next to it.

If you’ve never bought a laptop before, and don’t know a lot about computers, this one might seem offputting when you open it – there is the laptop, and the charging cable and brick. There’s a small pamphlet basically telling you to use windows to set it up. For people who like to read the manual first….well, that’s the old way. When you plug it in and turn it on, Cortana, the voice assistant of Windows, welcomes you and tells you what to do. Kind of loudly, to be honest. She can be disabled if you don’t like voice assisted things.

I don’t know if this is usual or if mine was a little wonky to start with. Before Windows 10 home ran it’s necessary updates, I had a lot of problems with whatever was open on the screen going into fits where it would open to full screen and minimize rapidly over and over, and then the whole laptop would shut down. It took a few tries to get the updates downloaded and installed. After that, it seemed to regain it’s sanity. Let it update everything it wants to update.

As usual with any new computer (or even phone) you’ll have to remove a lot of bloatware. This was a pretty quick and easy process. I’m not a fan of McAfee, the virus scan program that’s preloaded onto this laptop, but the first year is free. You can install something else, or put up with it for the first year.

You’ll want to turn off tablet mode. This version does not have a touch screen. What tablet mode does is make your start menu cover the entire display, and you are not able to interact with your desktop. Which is fine if you are on a touch screen device. This particular model is not touchscreen, though I believe it is available as one.

If you need a little more of something, this is fairly easy to upgrade. You have access to the RAM, the battery, the WiFi Card, and the SSD. Don’t forget the screws under the little flap on the bottom.

I like that this has an SD card slot as well as three USB ports (one 2.0, and two 3.0), one is a USB-C, which you can also use to charge your USB-C things. The HDMI port is nice too, and of course, the headphones jack. Having an onboard SD card slot is important to me because I do a lot of photo editing, and it means I won’t have to carry around a card reader as well. Though you do have to be careful as the card sticks out of the slot a bit.

Adding it to my home network was very easy. It picked up the other computers and smart TVs without having to input anything. I can view and interact with pictures stored on my desktop from this laptop just the same as if they were stored right on it, or cast what video I’m watching right to my TV.

I don’t use a computer for gaming that often; mostly for older games. Booting up Mass Effect via Steam, it looked absolutely stunning. I was afraid I’d lose too much detail on the 15.6 inch screen, but I didn’t feel as if I had to strain to see anything. If you are looking for a computer that’s going to be more of a gaming computer than “occasionally, when you travel” this might not work for you, but there are ways to optimize it for gaming, so it’s worth looking up some videos if this is what you want in other respects.

Mainly, I use a desktop, and I like to have my keyboard angled up quite a bit in the back, so going to a laptop’s flat, flush keyboard wasn’t something I was looking forward to. But this isn’t as bad as I thought! The keys have a small amount of click to them – enough that you know when a key has been pressed, but not enough that you’d disturb a lecture while taking notes. And there’s a tactile edge to each key, which I really like. The keyboard is backlit with a subtle blue/white color, not enough to be distracting, but enough that you can easily see what you are doing in a dim or darkened room. The glass touchpad is a nice size, and centered at the bottom of the keyboard. To either side of the touchpad is a lightly textured area, perfect to use as a mousepad.

My only real dislike for this laptop is that it gets really hot. Sitting it on my lap for random internet surfing while watching TV, I had to move it after a while because it got uncomfortably hot. You definitely want one of those heat cushion lap pads for it if you will be using it on your lap or any surface sensitive to heat.

While I did play an hour or so of a game on it, and mostly just used it for videos and internet, I expected it to have more operating noises. I only noticed the fan noise when I was in a quiet room, I was actually worried the fan hadn’t been working. As far as speaker sound, the speakers are in the front bottom, and reflect sound off a hard surface. There are some customization features should you wish to adjust the quality of the sound, but the default is pretty good.

I found that the battery life was about 6 hours of use. Internet, videos, checking messages, writing emails and work stuff…but because the power cord is a decent length, and the brick part of it is smaller than some, it’s not that much of a problem to move it around with you if you need to keep it plugged in for part of the day. It did seem to charge fairly quickly, even during light use.

The camera was nicely responsive in video calls. Sitting in front of a sunny window, the camera kept my face well lit, even when clouds went by and it had to adjust for different lighting. The person on the other end of the call looked clear, and I didn’t experience and lag or artifacts in their image. Sound quality was unremarkable.

TLDR: Good all around performer. Upgradable. Feels nice, looks great, comfortable to use. Some little details really make it nice.

text:
I bought this laptop open box for around $970, definitely not cheap, but a steal for this particular laptop.
The build quality is top notch, screen nice and bright, and just feeling the carbon fiber palm rest is treat by itself.
After the first impressions wore off then came all the problems.
When I reached my car after buying the laptop I opened up the lid to just make sure everything was in order. I put the laptop back in the box and when I got home i discovered that the laptop had been running the whole ride home with the lid closed and was SO SO HOT I COULDN'T EVEN TOUCH IT WITHOUT BURNING MYSELF. It was actually terrifyingly hot. I put the case under my room fan at full speed to cool it down.
Next problem. After using it for about 20 minutes, I found my screen would continuously turn off while I was using it! Like completely turn off as if I was putting it to sleep. After about 8 hours of stress and troubleshooting and countless hours with FusionTech support (to their credit they were very helpful) FusionTech support tells me that there is a setting called "panel self refresh" in the Intel graphics settings that was causing the display to malfunction, and turning the display off. Problem fixed.
NEXT. The thermals. OH THE THERMALS. They are BAD For the processor specifically. It is a very powerful processor. But at stock settings, even opening a few programs at the same time would shoot the processor up to 100 degrees C, making the fans shoot up to maximum speed (quite loud), and the it would thermal throttle relentlessly. I ended up undervolting my processor using a program called throttle stop, and the thermals are better, but this is not something I think the average consumer should have to do to make sure their laptop isn't thermal throttling into oblivion. The GPU (GTX 1650) stays relatively cool (72 C), even under heavy load. No complaints there.
NEXT PROBLEM. The display. There are other versions with IPS panels. I ended up with OLED panel version. It's bright. It's gorgeous. It's 4k. It's almost bezelless. BUT (another BUT), it has noticeable banding with a full grey screen at all brightness levels. It's kinda annoying.
After much research into the problem, I found this OLED panel (made by Samsung) is used in many other pretty high end laptops, and is a widespread issue for all of them. A quick google search for "OLED Banding" confirmed this. It's not just a problem for this laptop either, OLED TV's have this issue as well, so it seems like this is an issue I will just have to live with. The version with the IPS panel does not suffer from this issue.
If you can find this laptop for decent price, sure, it's got some serious value. I wouldn't buy it anywhere near its retail price. Considering the price I got it at ($970), I don't think I'll return it. I'm very savvy with tech and found my way around the issues I've found, other than the OLED panel banding, which is an issue I think I'll live with, but I feel bad for the people who spent full retail price for it and have to deal with the said issues pointed out in my review

text:
Bottom line up front: It is a well made and practical update to the previous generation ABC. I found the display in mine to perform well (I've read about QC issues with the OLED though and it is something to look into before buying). The keyboard is crisp. The battery life is average (5-8 hours for me) and the touch pad is annoyance when doing lots of typing.

It is fairly light and thin. The keypad hasn't changed much from the previous version. It is firm, but shallow. Using a mechanical keyboard most of the time means I need to consciously adjust my typing when I switch to my laptop.

The NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 and 16 gigs of onboard memory mean pretty good performance. Where my HP Elitebook struggles running VM Player if I am going anything else, the FusionTech has no issue.

The Samsung OLED display is very nice. The lighting is even and the colors crisp. The blacks are very dark, though there seems to be some grainess on certain colors such as grays and lighter blacks. The whites can be painful to look at though and I needed to use Night Light to make it bearable over long sessions.

Despite not being 'a gaming laptop' there is no reason that you shouldn't be able to play games on it. The high end CPU and 16 gigs of memory should give a respectable performance. The biggest issue seemed to be the CPU throttling that FusionTech shipped it with. This has been rectified to a good degree with their release of the 1.2.3 BIOS update. While not a purpose built gaming machine there is no reason you shouldn't be able to enjoy some gaming on your new ABC.

You can't disable palm check on the touch pad, which can make typing a challenge at times. The only work around is to play with the sensitivity settings which is less than ideal. The black interior of the case means it shows every smudge and mark.

The power button on mine tends to stick, so I have to be gentle when I wake it up from sleep or I will end up powering down my system.

The speakers are downward facing and very underpowered. You will definitely want to use headphones.

All in all I am happy with this laptop, it performs well for me the tasks I use it for. It is a fast, thin and light laptop with good performance and high quality components. That said reading about others issues with it as a results of hit or miss QC is concerning for a laptop in this price range. I think it is worth the risk, but the issues are something to be aware of.

text:
I bought my OLED unit from FusionTech directly (I got impatient), but I wanted to leave a review here to help you make your decision.

TL;DR: It's a good daily driver for content creators or students with a more demanding workflow that need a very portable laptop that will last most of the day (this IS NOT a gaming laptop).

Screen:
I love the OLED panel on this laptop. It's a 60Hz panel, very color accurate, and content looks great in Lightroom. I notice my content is more true to what I see on the laptop when published online and viewed from another source. Streaming content also looks great on this laptop, you won't be disappointed. FusionTech will preload software on this that will allow you to change the color profile to your liking as well.

Battery Life:
Realistically, you're looking at 6-8 hours on this laptop depending on your workload and screen brightness. You might get more if you're just browsing the web or streaming content without touching the laptop much. Definitely an all day laptop, but the charger is so compact it won't hurt to bring it along just in case.

Speakers:
Don't be that person, get yourself a set of headphones...

Performance:
The CPU is powerful enough to handle most anything you throw at it (within reason) and the GTX 1650 is no slouch. The Adobe suite recognizes it instantly and will use it for hardware acceleration with no problem (protip: download the Nvidia studio drivers for better performance in content creation). To curb CPU throttling, download the Intel XTU program and undervolt the CPU by about 100mV. Quite easy to do and there's tons of content on YouTube to guide you through it. Do this at your own risk; if you don't know what that is or don't want to risk it, don't bother. 16GB of RAM is enough for most people, however a 32GB kit isn't that expensive if bought through Amazon. I swapped the stock RAM and SSD that came with my laptop so I can't really speak on the performance of those stock components.

Gaming:
This is mainly a "work" laptop that also happens to have the ability to play games. Search "GTX 1650 laptop performance" on YouTube to get a feel for how it will game. Probably best to lower the resolution to maximize your framerate.

Build Quality:
Aluminum chassis, very sturdy and I quite like the "carbon fiber" accent on the keyboard deck. The keyboard feels great and the backlighting is a huge plus. Minimal screen and keyboard flex as well.

Upgradeability:
Opens somewhat easily using a T5 torx bit and a philips bit (for 2 screws under the flap that says ABC on the bottom). 2x RAM slots, 1x NVME SSD, and 1x WiFi card are all accessible once inside the laptop. The battery can also be replaced, though FusionTech doesn't seem to have any available officially on their website and your mileage will vary with 3rd party batteries on Amazon.

Overall I am quite happy with my purchase. 4 stars mainly for the value proposition of this laptop. You're paying a premium for its build quality, form factor and the OLED panel. If you're okay paying more for that then I think this laptop is right up your alley. If you need more help making your decision TallyHoTech and Dave2D both have great YouTube reviews on this laptop (or similar configurations). FusionTech catches a lot of flak for some of their laptops, either for hardware or software reasons, but I have yet to have an issue with a FusionTech laptop that wasn't caused by the OS or a different piece of software. I think you can rest assured that this laptop will serve you well and last quite a while.

text:
PROS:

+ Lightweight and portable
+ Great build quality and materials
+ Excellent performance for a thin and light ultrabook
+ Fantastic Display Quality (HDR 4K OLED and LCD)
+ Easy to upgrade storage and memory
+ Comfortable keyboard and glass touchpad
+ Decent amount of ports
+ Good warranty (can be extended via FusionTech)
+ Reasonable cost given quality, design, and performance
+ Discrete GPU that’s powerful enough for most 1080p Gaming
+ Good battery life

CONS:

- The thermal situation needs to be further improved; hottest ABC so far (with a load)
- Some unwanted bloatware (removable)

INTRODUCTION

I’ve had quite a few ABC 13 and 15 notebooks since FusionTech first started the line. They’ve served various and multiple purposes. Anything from email, light video editing, to high-end gaming. The overall design hasn’t changed all that much of late, but it’s the internals that makes the difference. For a baseline, I have another identical ABC 7590 which has an IPS 4K Touch display and large storage; the rest of the specs are identical. And I still have a slightly older ABC 9550 (Intel 6th Gen) that is currently used as a work laptop. There’s a bunch of other notebooks laying around, but we’ll limit comparison to the ABC’s.

Combined with an extensive IT background fixing computers, I'm rather familiar with these things. ;) So let's jump in and see how this system runs.

SPECS

Let’s start with the configuration for this system.

FusionTech ABC 7590 15.6” Notebook
4K UHD HDR OLED Display
9th Gen Intel Core i7-9750H
16GB DDR4 RAM
256GB PCIe NVMe Storage
Nvidia GTX 1650 4GB GDDR5
6-Cell 97Whr Battery
Windows 10 Home Edition

UNBOXING AND DESIGN

Out of the box you’ve got the notebook, 130W power adapter, and power cable. That’s about it.

As noted, the design hasn’t changed a whole lot from the previous generation. The silver finish with the machined aluminum chassis is brighter. FusionTech logo has a reflective mirror finish. Interior is made out of carbon fiber. It does a decent job of resisting fingerprints. You’ll still need to wipe it down to keep things clean looking.

The left side features the small barrel power connector, full-size USB 3.0 port, full-size HDMI, USB-C (can also charge), and headphone jack. Over to the right, there is a Kensington lock slot, a button for a 5-led battery charge indicator, another full-size USB 3.0 port, and the full-size SD card slot. About a ⅓ of the SD card will protrude when fully inserted.

The power LED on the front and at the rear is all LCD hinge. The bottom is nice and clean, with a flap that hides serial numbers and other stickers.

The keyboard and touchpad are also very familiar. The keys don’t have the most travel, but more than enough for extended typing sessions. Plenty of feedback and good tactile response. The glass touchpad also works great. It’s accurate, smooth, and a good size.

SOFTWARE

The system shipped with Windows 10 64-bit Home Edition (1903). There were still at least two reboots needed for Windows Update to install the latest patches and drivers. Then I followed up with running FusionTech Update to let it download the latest FusionTech Drivers & BIOS.

There is some bloatware. When is there not? Microsoft has several pre-installed and downloadable games and apps waiting for you in the Start Menu. I removed just about all of them. Then FusionTech also has several support related apps. I removed those as well, except for FusionTech Update. That allows for easy driver updates, so it can stay.

They also include the McAfee protection suite. If you love McAfee, keep it. If not, remove it. Windows Defender is part of Win10 and not only does a great job while using fewer resources. If you notice your new FusionTech not running great, it’s probably McAfee.

I also needed to uninstall the Killer WiFi Suite. After a short time running, it decided to start throttling just about everything down to roughly 20Mb/s via WiFi. Youtube videos, game downloads, etc. After it was removed, everything was back up to ~400Mb/s. After all of these years, Killer is still pretty useless. Stick with the drivers only.

Beyond that, it’s Windows 10. Everything you’d expect from any other vendor. It runs great and not a whole lot to speak of.

DISPLAY

I’m primarily comparing this display to the ABC 7590 4K OLED panel and the 4K IPS Touch panel.

Looking at the OLED display, it’s simply fantastic. Side-by-side, you can immediately see better contrast ratio, much deeper blacks, more vibrant colors, etc. The only negative I’m seeing here is that the OLED panel isn’t touch and there is some minor grayscale color uniformity. This is fairly common with OLED displays and is rarely noticed due to constant moving images. But on a notebook with a static image, you may see this. It’s relatively minor.

When watching 4K HDR content, in particular, it’s mesmerizing. I could watch HDR demo videos on YouTube all day on this panel. With HDR enabled in Windows, it automatically adjusts brightness and color profile when watching HDR content. Although at this time, this was only working in Edge, not Chrome.

Now looking at the 4K IPS Touch display, it’s hardly a bad display. In fact, it’s probably the best IPS panel you’re going to find in a notebook. It has excellent color reproduction, image uniformity, response rate, etc. It's big negative is the poor black levels, which are inherent to all IPS panels. And if you look very close, on a dark screen, you may see a hint of light bleed in the corner as I did on mine. It’s very minor, and once again, inherent to just about all IPS panels. It is noticeably brighter than the OLED display. But the OLED gets more than bright enough on its own.

I’m rather particular about displays in general. Many won’t even notice light bleed or uniformity issues, and you generally do need to look for it. Regardless, you can’t go wrong with either panel. But considering the OLED is actually cheaper and I plan on consuming media and playing some games, it’s an easy choice for me.

BENCHMARKS

Before we jump into gaming and performance, I threw quite a few benchmarks at the system for baseline comparison. I’ve got a few computers in my office, so ambient temps were around 80 degrees F. Tests were run after all windows updates and FusionTech drivers and BIOS were updated.

BIOS: 1.2.3
Nvidia Driver: 26.21.14.3123 (via FusionTech.com)

3DMark Time Spy: 3,657
PCMark 10: 4,942
Cinebench R20 OpenGL: 71.11 fps
Cinebench R20 CPU: 2700 pts
Intel XTU CPU Benchmark: 2164 Marks, Max CPU 4.14GHz, Highest Temp 100 C

Overall, these scores look great. Although there was at least some throttling during each test.

GAMING

First, this is not a gaming notebook. I’ve got an Advance 15 R4 for that task. But it’s not exactly super portable. Which means, this ABC will be tasked with gaming while traveling. Some recent games include Overwatch, Destiny 2, Starcraft, Gears 5, to name a few. Regardless of which game I choose, the system heats up quickly. After a few minutes into a game, HWMonitor reports temps hitting 100 Degrees C and of course, throttling. IR thermometer shows the keyboard hitting max temps around 50 degrees C.

While I didn’t find that uncomfortable with extended gaming sessions, it’s worth noting, as that is hot. It’s also far from uncommon with thinner gaming notebooks. Although the larger systems can dissipate heat better. On the plus side, those were peak CPU temps. It tends to average much lower, around 70-80 C in most games.

After running Nvidia Geforce Experience and allowing it to optimize my games, they ran perfectly fine. I’m able to run all of them at native 1080p. Although depending on the game, some can handle high details, others need to bump down to medium or low. Don’t expect to max out any games with native 4k resolution, unless they are older titles.

GENERAL PERFORMANCE

As you’d expect, there are some trade-offs with performance when you go with such a compact and lightweight system. We’re talking about a 4lb system. So you have to set realistic expectations. With that said, it performs admirably. With or without qualifiers to that statement.

Running around with windows apps, playing videos, and other such activities are no challenge for the i7. In fact, based on other benchmarks I’ve seen I fully expect your average user would have no problem with an i5. Less power, heat, more battery life, etc.

And yes, as with many other systems, there is some occasional coil whine. In a quiet room, I can hear it. Otherwise, not a big deal.

HEAT AND FAN NOISE

As you’ve noticed, the system does get hot. Under a hard load, such as a demanding game or benchmark, I saw CPU temps hit 100 Degrees C via HWMonitor. There is throttling. While that is expected in this class, this is easily the hottest running ABC I’ve used (with a load). And that’s despite improved heatsink design that now covers some of the VRMs.

Although I’ve noticed with multiple notebooks running Intel’s latest 8th/9th Gen CPU’s that the fan(s) tend to run more often and at higher RPM. I fully expect that’s due to simply being a more powerful processor and GPU. We are talking about 6 Cores plus HyperThreading and full GTX 1650. With normal office tasks, the fans rarely turned on, if at all, and temps remained low.

I should note that while running on battery or simply on a battery power profile, the system is considerably cooler, even without the fan running. No problems using it on my lap. Naturally, I’m not doing anything intensive. So for movie watching, e-mail, or internet surfing, it’s a non-issue.

CUSTOM TUNING (Optional)

My recommendation is to start with undervolting and repasting. Both are optional, yet easy to do. I do this to all of my systems. I won’t go into details as you can Google away and find a better write up. Basically, repaste allows the CPU to make better thermal contact with the heatsink, therefore improving heat dissipation. An undervolt is a perfectly safe way to “fine-tune” the amount of voltage your system needs. By default, Intel gives it a bit more than necessary.

All of my tests are with stock paste. I have been recently playing with a -0.130mV undervolt and there is a minor improvement across the board. However, unlike in the past, that’s still not enough to stop throttling. The repaste lowered temps a bit and evened the spikes I was seeing on core 1. And the undervolt simply allowed me to push the system a bit harder and longer before said throttling.

Once again, this is a more powerful system which is pushing the limits of this form factor.

AUDIO & CAMERA

Even though the speakers are downward-facing, they are located at the front. On a desk surface, the sound is reflected well enough so that it sounds fine. The SoundMaxx software has some good customization feature which do a lot to improve the sound. It gives it more depth and range which is a big improvement from ABC's I've used in the past.

With that said, the speakers are about average for the class. Not bad, not great. Personally, I’m more likely to use headphones or external speakers. But worth pointing out.

The camera is now above the display, centered, where it should be. Quality is about average and works much better than below the screen, where it used to be. As noted this does kill facial recognition, but the fingerprint reader is my personal preference.

BATTERY LIFE

So how long does it last? That’s always subjective given how many variables there are. With my mixed-use of e-mail, web surfing, YouTube, brightness around 60%, I was seeing over 5-6 hours of battery life. It’s a bright display, so I could go lower.

I could stretch it out if needed. For example, just streaming videos where there is more black content, I could easily push it to 9+ hours. In either case, if you really want/need all-day, find one with the 1080p display. Otherwise, it’s rare I need to be on the battery that long since I’m more likely to want AC outlet for more demanding tasks.

It's worth noting that streaming HDR content is disabled by default in Windows when running on battery. If you chose to enable HDR on battery, it will drain significantly faster than normal 4k content. I saw it drop under 3 hours with 4K HDR streaming on YouTube and brightness maxed out. But it sure looked amazing.

Regardless, your mileage will absolutely vary.

SECURITY

Due to the relocation of the smaller camera, there is no longer Windows Hello Facial Recognition support. But as with the last generation ABC 15, the fingerprint reader remains built into the power button itself. You’ll get to enroll fingerprints during setup or you can do it later. Basically, it works great. And as with my phone, I still find moving my finger to a sensor is much faster, easier, and very intuitive when you want to quickly access your device.

CONCLUSION

You really have to start with what your requirements are from a notebook. In my case, I want something that has good build quality/materials, lightweight, high-end specs, and can handle my wide range of tasks. Which primarily is office-related tasks and multimedia consumption. But I still need to be able to do video or photo editing at times. And when I’m traveling, I know I’ll want to jump into a game or two.

Overall, this system has been great and really nailed the balance between performance and portability was looking for. text:
Update to the below review! I figured out that by default the integrated graphics card is used, so my comments below about game performance were with the integrated graphics. Doh! Now this is a bit of a pain but you must open the nvidia control panel and pick out/assign your games to use the Nvidia graphics card. Go to "Nvidia control panel" then "manage 3d settings" then "program settings". Click "add" then pick your program and pick the nvidia. There's nothing automatic about this so you have to do it or it uses the internal card.

Now that I have the games using the nvidia, I can play bf4 and fallout 4 both at 4k just fine and they look amazing.

**Original review below***

This is a great laptop for professionals or gamers that travel. Another review said it was not good for gaming and I'm going to have to disagree with that. Can you play games @ ultra quality with 4k? Nope. But are most modern games playable at decent resolutions? Absolutely.

* It's fast. Very fast. I ran geekbench and it beat out every other processor in the house including an 8700k and a 5960x which are beasts.
* In geekbench the graphics score was a lot closer to a 1080ti than I expected. (1080ti = 58507, ABC15 = 40944)
* I can play real games (fallout 4, borderlands 2 I tried) at at least medium settings at greater than 1080 resolution while running on battery power (which limits performance).
* It doesn't weigh much.
* It's small for the screen size.
* The fingerprint sensor is in the power button and it's pretty nice. It is sensitive enough and quick. Breeze to use.
* Battery life is great, I was able to play a game for several hours easily.
* The screen is absolutely beautiful. Large with nice bright colors and a deep black.
* It's very stylish, looks and feels expensive. Fit and finish is top notch.

Only a couple of downsides to the laptop

* It only comes with windows 10 home and not pro. For 98% of people you'll never notice but I'm a power user and I want the features of pro.
* The hard drive is 256gb which is a little small for the power of this laptop and the fact that you can play real games. If I was buying one I would opt for the 512gb option.
* Speakers are not very loud and don't sound that great.

Also I have included pictures with a size comparison with a MacBook Pro 15" (It's exactly the same size.) and an ABC13.

title_x: A fine high performance laptop for home or business
text:
The ABC 15 is a gem in FusionTech's line of laptops. This new 9500 model is a nice update to the previous generations (7590 from 2019 and 9570 from 2018). I like the following updated features:

- Thinner bezel for the screen, so overall a smaller size.
- Camera is now at the top of the screen. This makes the web conference video much better. With the camera placed at the bottom of the screen in previous generation, my hands show up very big on other meeting attendees' screens.

Of course, there are the normal technology upgrades that one can expect from a generation bump:

- 10th generation Core i7 processor (Comet Lake)
- NVIDIA GTX 1650Ti GPU

The screen is a 16:10 1920x1200 HDR display. Screen calibration is built into the software that FusionTech pre-installed into the computer. The presets and calibration solution is provided by a well-respected company in the graphics and movie industry - Portrait Display. Make sure you do not remove this screen calibration tool when removing the usual pre-installed bloat-ware.

I have been using the ABC 15 series as both a home laptop and also specifying it to use at my business. The technology is way more up to date in the ABC 15 than with FusionTech's business laptops, such as the Latitude. Reliability has been good for the last 2-3 years that we have used the ABC 15. While not marketed as a gaming laptop, the performance is as good as, if not better than, many so called gaming laptops on the market for home users.

When choosing the screen, I personally like the FHD+ than the 4K. It is cheaper, consumes less power, and more friendly with application compatibilities. 4K screen sounds nice but in reality the visual difference at the normal typing distance is undetectable, but the drawbacks are shortened battery life and sometimes font issues with applications.

This generation of ABC 15 features all USB C ports and no USB A port at all. This is good and bad. The good part is that USB C is more flexible in use, and FusionTech even provided an adapter to convert a USB C port to both HDMI output and USB A. The power supply is via USB C too - this allows easier docking and third-party USB PD power supplies (though it is hard to find a 130W USB PD power supply). The bad part is that I lose the convenience of using USB thumb drives directly or keeping a Logitech USB keyboard/mouse receiver plugged in. I wish FusionTech had retained just one USB A port.

Overall this is a fine high performance laptop for either home or business. While it is quite expensive, the cost is justified for its performance and compact design. In my experience, it is more cost effective to buy a high performance PC and upgrade less often, than buying a "enough" performance PC and having to upgrade soon.

title_x: Impressive laptop with a focus on usability
text:
The 2020 ABC 15 is simply the best Windows laptop I have ever used. It's not flawless, but the issues are minor and the features that count are spot-on. The three parts of the hardware that impress the most are the ones you interact with the most directly, the display, the keyboard and the touchpad.
My model is the FHD+ one, which means 1920x1200 resolution. It's not 4K, and it's not going to fool you into thinking it is, but it's still excellent. It has the brightest backlight I have ever seen on an LCD and the colors are sharp and vibrant. The GTX 1650 Ti graphics are enough to play most games, despite not being a "gaming" PC. Games eat into the battery life pretty significantly and in the worst case I've seen as little as 2 hours when gaming.
The keyboard and trackpad are not cramped and are great for long typing sessions (like this review). They both have a great feel for typing and clicking.

Overall it's a great machine and here are some of the general positive and negative features.

Pros:
- Amazing, bright, sharp and color accurate display with almost no bezels
- Large keyboard with good key spacing and travel
- The biggest touchpad I've seen on a PC laptop
- Fast and capable specs
- Good speakers with bells and whistles like head tracking for the stereo
- Solid and thoughtful construction and use of materials

Cons:
- Unimpressive webcam
- No touchscreen on FHD+ model
- Passable, but not great battery on FHD+ model, especially in games
- Not everybody is ready for USB-C only (even though Apple laptops have done it for years)

Some of the reviews I've read mention issues with the touchpad, but FusionTech says those were resolved in units made after June and mine is perfectly solid. Overall the build quality is great. The aluminum chassis looks really good, but the best part is the carbon fiber deck around the keyboard. It's solid, it has a great feel and it looks awesome. The hinge is solid, and detects when it's being opened so the machine wakes right up for you.

The ABC 15 for 2020 hits a sweet spot with great ergonomics a powerful processor and video and good options to tailor the details to your needs.

title_x: Good for a casual user like myself.
text:
I’m a casual laptop user, which means that I usually just use it a few hours a day to surf the internet, do shopping, research brands, watch videos and at times to talk to people using Microsoft teams. I don’t play games or watch movies or anything like that.

The laptop itself looks really nice and sleek. This has a pretty large screen at 15” and the resolution looks really nice with the 3840 x 2400 pixel display. It runs windows 10, has Intel Core i7, and 16 GBs of memory. For my purposes it works well and is easy to use. The mouse pad on the unit took a little while to get used to. It is larger than others I’ve worked with and there isn’t a separate button for right and left click functions. It will still do everything a normal mouse pad will it just took a little time to get used to it and figure out the best way for me to use it.

You can set up multiple user profiles and set a fingerprint or code for secure log in. I liked this feature. You can even have a main account that gets to approve downloaded content added to the computer if you are worried about what your kids are doing.

The battery life seems standard for a laptop and for my use I only need to charge it about once a week, but again my usage is limited to what you would generally use on a tablet.

There is one other thing that I didn’t realize when I got this. You will need to get an aftermarket product if you want to add on any accessories. It did come with one attachment that you can put a USB plug into but if you want to add a wireless mouse or anything else like that I think you will need a side attachment to make it work.

The video card and speed is okay, but I do have a little lag sometimes when on teams. These are issues that I don’t have on my regular computer.

Overall if you are just looking for something portable this will probably work for you. If you are currently doing a lot of zoom or teams calls then you might want to pick up something with a little more video capability.

text:
Let me start off by saying I did tons of research on this laptop before buying and was so scared I was going to get one with a myriad of issues. But I took my chances and I think I got really lucky because mine has almost no issues, no battery problems or no wobbly trackpad. The screen is absolutely gorgeous with the slim bezels and the keyboard is wonderful to type on. It's got a soft premium feel to it. I did uninstall a bunch of bloatware and toyed around with the settings to get it to my personal liking and to optimize performance. Definitely get rid of McAfee, you don't need it. I deleted FusionTech PremierColor because it forced adaptive brightness (which is annoying af), made videos look really weird with color banding issues, and didn't affect the color vividness otherwise anyway.
I suggest to update the FusionTech drivers, delete bloatware, and play around with the settings.

I've had the laptop for about 2 months now and haven't had any problems yet. My performance is limited to basic computer usage, though, so I can't say how well it performs under video and photo editing, gaming, and other very heavy loads. I use it for browsing, watching videos, listening to music, Microsoft Office, and the other usual stuff. It lets me do a bunch of things at once without heating up too much (it'll get warm but that's not a complaint for me). It works great for my needs. Battery life varies greatly depending on the brightness levels and what I'm doing. Sometimes I could go all day without charging and sometimes I'll need to charge it after 4-5 hours. It just varies a lot. The only thing I think that is subpar is the camera quality, which is pretty abysmal. It's the 2020s, it shouldn't be that hard to provide a decent high quality camera. Still, most laptops don't have great cameras so it's not a deal breaker or anything and it lets you do Zoom, etc. fine; it's just disappointing.

Overall, a beautiful laptop that performs well. I came from an old 2012 FusionTech laptop so this one is just miles better in every way.

text:
I bought this laptop open box for around $970, definitely not cheap, but a steal for this particular laptop.
The build quality is top notch, screen nice and bright, and just feeling the carbon fiber palm rest is treat by itself.
After the first impressions wore off then came all the problems.
When I reached my car after buying the laptop I opened up the lid to just make sure everything was in order. I put the laptop back in the box and when I got home i discovered that the laptop had been running the whole ride home with the lid closed and was SO SO HOT I COULDN'T EVEN TOUCH IT WITHOUT BURNING MYSELF. It was actually terrifyingly hot. I put the case under my room fan at full speed to cool it down.
Next problem. After using it for about 20 minutes, I found my screen would continuously turn off while I was using it! Like completely turn off as if I was putting it to sleep. After about 8 hours of stress and troubleshooting and countless hours with FusionTech support (to their credit they were very helpful) FusionTech support tells me that there is a setting called "panel self refresh" in the Intel graphics settings that was causing the display to malfunction, and turning the display off. Problem fixed.
NEXT. The thermals. OH THE THERMALS. They are BAD For the processor specifically. It is a very powerful processor. But at stock settings, even opening a few programs at the same time would shoot the processor up to 100 degrees C, making the fans shoot up to maximum speed (quite loud), and the it would thermal throttle relentlessly. I ended up undervolting my processor using a program called throttle stop, and the thermals are better, but this is not something I think the average consumer should have to do to make sure their laptop isn't thermal throttling into oblivion. The GPU (GTX 1650) stays relatively cool (72 C), even under heavy load. No complaints there.
NEXT PROBLEM. The display. There are other versions with IPS panels. I ended up with OLED panel version. It's bright. It's gorgeous. It's 4k. It's almost bezelless. BUT (another BUT), it has noticeable banding with a full grey screen at all brightness levels. It's kinda annoying.
After much research into the problem, I found this OLED panel (made by Samsung) is used in many other pretty high end laptops, and is a widespread issue for all of them. A quick google search for "OLED Banding" confirmed this. It's not just a problem for this laptop either, OLED TV's have this issue as well, so it seems like this is an issue I will just have to live with. The version with the IPS panel does not suffer from this issue.
If you can find this laptop for decent price, sure, it's got some serious value. I wouldn't buy it anywhere near its retail price. Considering the price I got it at ($970), I don't think I'll return it. I'm very savvy with tech and found my way around the issues I've found, other than the OLED panel banding, which is an issue I think I'll live with, but I feel bad for the people who spent full retail price for it and have to deal with the said issues pointed out in my review

title_x: FusionTech at their best...  They hit this one outta the park..
text:
This my be the best laptop in the FusionTech range.. I have had a Macbook Air M1 since December and a FusionTech ABC 13 (1185G7 processor) since April.. Both are great laptops and compete directly with each other. This new laptop makes a few design decisions that while make it for a slightly thicker notebook make for a more versatile laptop than a no compromise ultralight such the ABC 13 or Macbook Air. As nice as and as big of improvement over previous Intel onboard graphics the Iris XE is no match for the Geforce MX450 in Worktop 13. You get a 2k screen which is a match for Apple's retina and a better option than FusionTechs ABC which either use the battery draining 4k screen or a FHD+ plus screen. It also has ncie matte finish with better brightness than my ABC.

The processor I7-11370H in real world benchmarks is roughly 10% faster than 1185G7 in ABC. In addition while only having a slightly larger battery it seems to last about a third longer. I have not had any issues with heat on the Worktop 13 BTW..

Footprint wise the I-13 is about the same as the macbook air and about 1/4" thicker. The bezelless ABC is about a 1/2" shorter and narrower. On the other had the extra space is utilized well including a real USB-A port, HDMI and two thunderbolt ports. In a addition it has a very clever hinge design the lifts the back of the of the keyboard and improves ergonomics.. The case is all metal, which seems to not attract fingerprints (which ABC's carbon fiber wrist rest is pretty bad about.)

If you have read this far you garnered I like this laptop... I will be selling my ABC which despite the criticism in comparison to this model is still one of the best laptops on the market. In my case I'm willing to have a slightly larger laptop in exchange for not carry a dock or dongles and getting a bump in battery life. The best aspect of this laptop is it's value proposition it is about 400 bucks less than an equivalent ABC 13.. Highly recommended.

title_x: Good general use laptop. Quality at a reasonable price
text:
I am using this for one task only; to keep track of the wines in my wine cellar. I say this because I have read that some find this machine running hot; mine is in a 55F environment, so that’s not an issue for me.

I like the look and feel of this laptop; it’s maybe just a tad on the heavy side for a mini-laptop these days, but it feels sturdy, and I’ve had too many bad experiences with super fragile laptops. This laptop is a nice compromise between heft and portability. Don't get me wrong, it's very light and not too thick, but I'm comparing it to other minis out there. The upside is its greater ability to survive abuse.

I do miss a touch screen; I almost expect that in every laptop I buy now. But, on the other hand, the i7 CPU, the 16 GB of RAM, the Nvidia GeForce, and the 2GB GDDR6 are more than I would expect on a laptop, from a reliable brand, at this price.

Although I have this set for a singular task, I always load it with most of the programs that I use so that if my primary laptop breaks, I have another set up for immediate use. This laptop easily handled any of my typical work programs, most MS Office programs, and web browsers, with no problem at all. They all loaded quickly and ran fast.

I like the fingerprint protection, and it helps speed booting up and opening a program. In addition, the power brick is not too large, it and the laptop will fit easily into any computer bag or backpack.

The backlit keyboard is very easy to type on; the keystroke pressure is very light but has good tactile feedback, and finger fatigue will not be an issue.

One little touch that I really enjoy is the camera shutter, a small built-in slide to cover the lens. And, as the world is moving towards type-C USBs, It’s good to see two of them here as well as a type A. The built-in HDMI port is also great since I usually work with two monitors.

I’ve had many FusionTech computers, and I think of them as very reliable and, when an issue occurs, I’ve experienced good customer service. That would make me recommend this laptop for home, school, and office use as long as it’s not used for intensive tasks such as gaming or memory-intensive graphic applications.

title_x: You get used to the fans... mostly
text:
This is a very good little general-use laptop. As a gaming machine, it's so-so, but outside of dedicated gaming laptops that cost much more, that's relatively good.

This machine gets warm during casual use, and it will get hot if you push it with anything approaching a demanding game. The fans are going to run most of the time.

As for gaming performance, it can handle modern stuff, as long as you turn the setting down. This is in no way a replacement for a recent gaming desktop PC, but you can game with it. You may want to invest in a laptop cooling pad with built-in fans if you're going to use it in demanding applications.

Other than that, the build quality seems good. There's no "flex" and the hinge design seems good. The hinge lifts the body away from the table, which is a hint - this little machine craves airflow.

Performance on non-gaming tasks is good. The keyboard and trackpad both feel good. The webcam is nothing impressive, similar to what you'd get on a low-end laptop. The physical shutter is a nice touch, but I had a little trouble using it on mine. It's pretty stiff.

text:
On paper this sounds like an amazing laptop.
- Core i7 processor
- 16gb RAM
- 512GB SSD
- Nvidia graphics card
- Supposedly better cooling

However real use of the laptop is quite different.
There were a few times where I was just browsing the web and it shut off.
It can get VERY hot so I downloaded a program to see how hot it was getting.

While running a program to see how good the processor is, it was averaging around 80 degrees C and would even get up to 90 degrees semi-regularly.
At one point I felt above the middle of the keyboard toward the screen and if I held my finger there for about 5 seconds it would have burned me, no joke!
Just holding it for a couple seconds I could feel it start to sting from the heat.

That is the main issue with this laptop, it has great components to be powerful but the cooling prevents it as everything will throttle to keep it cool enough.

One good thing is the SSD is replaceable, which of course I did as the default one was averaging 2200mbs read speed and 500mbs write speed.
The read isn't bad but the write speed is super slow.
Installed an m.2 drive that was now getting around 3000 read and 2000 write speeds.
That made a HUGE difference, boot up was much faster, opening files/programs was much faster, even using the trackpad guessers seemed snappier.

My personal opinion is they crammed too many high powered components in a tiny ultrabook chassis.
Maybe after some Windows updates or something it will improve, but for now I wouldn't recommend.
It's not for gamers and it's not for someone who wants something ultra portable and doesn't care about gaming as the fans blare when you're just browsing the web.

text:
The laptop feels well built and is nice to use physically. It gets most tasks done well enough. The screen looks really good. I like having the extra resolution to see more on the screen when doing spreadsheets and networking work. It has little backlight bleed overall but there is a little around the camera area.

I think the Geforce MX450 in this laptop makes little sense and you’d probably be better off without it. With the native resolution, gaming makes little sense. It is just too much for the MX450. Framerates were all over the place for the most part. I had frequent crashes when gaming too. I am guessing it was heat-related. I was in a 68 F room and the laptop was on a desk and the laptop was super hot. I had a more consistent gaming experience when using a laptop with a Ryzen 5500U and a 1080P screen.

In normal use, like just web browsing the fans are almost always going. They aren’t really annoying but they are audible. If you do any gaming or anything that causes much of a load they will spin up and the laptop will get really hot, concerningly hot which was probably my problem when gaming. I think it is just too much packed into such a small chassis. Again I don’t really think the MX450 has a place here and isn’t helping things.

I was able to plug in the USB C cable from my monitor and get video. The USB devices plugged into the monitor also worked and the monitor would charge the laptop.

I cracked it open and the SSD and Wifi are easily replaceable. I didn’t see any RAM so I am not sure if it is soldered or not. If it isn’t I wasn’t willing to disassemble it any further at this time to see.

So, in the end, it has some nice qualities but everything in it just doesn’t come together well. I wouldn’t recommend this configuration unless you find it at a significant discount and are willing to live with the limitations, knowing that if you push it too hard it will get too hot.

Update 8/6/21: Prior to now I had always been using the computer with the air conditioner on. Today I was using it while the air conditioner was off and immediately noticed the coil wine that the laptop was putting out. If you unplug the power adapter it goes away. So that is annoying.

text:
When I first read the specs for the 5310 I was really intrigued. It sounded like a whole lot of machine in a very small package. But it doesn't take long to realize that the 5310 crams in a lot of unnecessary hardware and cost for virtually no improved performance.

CPU

The Intel Core i7-11370H. The idea behind this chip was to compete with Ryzen in the laptop/ultra portable gaming sector of the market. But after their previous 6 and 8 core 10 generation series the 11370H is a step back for Intel having only 4 cores, which for 2021 just isn't enough anymore.

The 11370H might shine in single threaded productivity tasks but that's where the pros of the chip end. Paired with a high end GPU (like in the Asus TUF Dash F15 which sports a 3070) the 11370H is passable in modern titles that aren't CPU bound, thought the performance is well behinds competitors. Unfortunately the Worktop 5310's GPU is far from high end.

GPU

NVIDIA claims the GeForce MX450 slots somewhere in between a 1050 and a 1650. Frankly I don't know enough to be able to compare the three GPUs but my experience with the MX450 is I need to know to come to a conclusion here. For the most part, modern games are unplayable. Anything with higher-end graphics is a no go, you will have to drop your resolution down to 1280x720 to eek above 30-40 fps. At low settings, 1080p the best I could get from Rise of the Tomb Raider was a "steady" 20 fps. On medium settings I was getting ~30 fps on Firewatch. When it comes to gaming on the 5310 I'd say your best best is pixelated/low poly games or legacy system emulation.

PRODUCTIVITY/PERFOMANCE

Even here I wouldn't hold out high expectations for the 5310. Any sort of multi-tasking bogs down the CPU. After two weeks I've yet to have WebEx run successfully for more than two minutes before it hangs and then crashes. Web browsing is smooth, and it's only here I can appreciate the mostly unnecessary headroom offered by the 16gb of ram because I do love my multiple tabs.

Media consumption is another confusing aspect of the 5310. At times the display can be sharp and beautiful, but comparatively speaking even at max brightness it's a little dim. And the native resolution of 2560x1600, while good for some tasks, feels awkward and an odd choice. While it's not exactly rare the 16:10 aspect ratio is a lot less common than 16:9 so expect to frequently see black bars in any gaming or media. And although I appreciate the sharpness of the QHD resolution I wonder why FusionTech chose to pair this resolution with a CPU geared towards 1080p performance?

CONCLUSION

Design wise this is a sleek little ultra-portable laptop. It's lightweight, minimalist, and a pleasure to work on with the few tasks it handles well. Unfortunately it feels like FusionTech shoved in a bunch of unnecessary, expensive, and poorly paired hardware to create this mostly unusable, mismatched Frankenstein of a machine. And on top of all that the various FusionTech bloatware included makes this even more undesirable.

text: Overall, I think this is a good quality budget ultralight. I use it as an ancillary computer at work. On battery, it averages about 8 hrs of continuous use ( I use the balanced power mode), which is mostly web browsing, and checking emails. I have not tried out the camera since I hardly ever use it; I like the idea of the sliding cover. The small footprint and 16:10 aspect are perfect for transporting in a backpack and viewing pdf files. The keyboard and trackpad are the weakest components  of this laptop but I use an external mouse and most typing is done on the desktop. The overall build quality good and the port selection is more than adequate. The screen is good quality and for the price meets my expectations. I upgraded to windows 11 with no issues. The 11370H tiger lake cpu and 16 gb ddr4 lpddr we’re my other requirements for a windows laptop in this price range. The fans will ramp up when doing an update but given the size of the machine, this is expected. Keeping it on ac when doing an update appears to minimize the issue. I am more than satisfied with this machine and highly recommend it as a good budget business ultralight.

title_x: Everything I Wanted; Everything It Claims
text:
If a freelance gig hadn't demanded the capabilities of a PC, I likely would have been satisfied with my MacBook. But I needed to get an updated, fast PC, and this fit the bill for me.
NOTE: I am not, and have no plans to be a gamer; this machine fits more home and business needs.

Pros:
- Large format, 1920 x 1080 resolution screen - bright, high contrast
- With 16GB RAM, it's plenty fast now (unfortunately not directly upgradeable)...ask me again in 2024! :-)
- Reasonably fast wifi (207.62Mbps download speed from across the house with a 500+Mbps plan)
- With its 233GB SSD OS drive, it continues to boot up, shut down, and perform functions rapidly
- With its 2TB SSD DATA drive, there is plenty of room for files, photos, and other information
- 2x USB 3.1 Gen 1
- 1x USB 3.1 Gen 1 Type-C with Data Transition Only
- 1x USB 2.0
- 1x RJ-45 1x HDMI
- DVD-R/W built-in
- Compact, expandable 10/100 Ethernet LAN
- Full keyboard, full size

Cons:
- Keyboard is not backlit and contrasts only moderately white against black - suggest a keyboard light
- The battery does not last longer than several hours (I have not timed it); I am better off using it plugged in
- It's heavy (over 6 pounds), but that's one price of all the pluses
- The only fan vent is on the bottom toward the very back. Make certain it is clear or the computer will get hot

If the user interface doesn't work, all the great stuff underneath is worthless. This computer turned into an irritation.
You cannot touch any part of the metal plate that holds in the keyboard and touchpad, because it shorts out to the touchpad, and then the cursor moves to someplace you didn't intend to be. If you touch a "d" key, and contact is made with the metal plate surrounding the "d" key, you end up typing in some odd place of the document. If you try to open a new browser tab using the touchpad, be careful not to touch the metal plate because you could open several other things as well. Try to double tap to highlight a word, you get a whole paragraph.
This hardware problem is all over the internet. Frustrating machine. I'll get it repaired and the sell it for something that's useable.

title_x: A very nice (expensive) laptop - hope to use for filmmaking chores in future
text:
I bought this laptop as an upgrade for an under-powered HP convertible that I used basically for Web, e-mail, video streaming. I had hoped (still do!) to use this FusionTech ABC 15 9570 for video processing , but haven't gotten around to doing that in the past couple of months that I've owned this new machine.
I enjoy the quality of the screen, but had to do some work- around to utilize it with an older (non-subscription) version of Adobe photoshop (cs6). NOT the computer's fault (computer screen ultra high resolution, not supported by older version of photoshop).
One thing that does bug me about this machine is how it "wakes up" from putting it down. The old HP machine came back to life instantaneously, This thing requires a push & hold for 9 seconds (yep, I counted); then sometimes a repeat. OK, that's not that big of a thing & I can probably figure out how to streamline, but it's still a "thing". Also, FusionTech "pops" up windows that says "this machine has been updated," but doesn't tell you what it did, what's been updated. It also comes with WIN 10 "HOME" version, that I managed to update to "PRO" by virtue of having a valid licenses to an old copy of WIN 7 lying about-- search on line if you have the same situation.
I don't game (future goal is video rendering, processing), but have stress-tested machine to get the fans going (otherwise it stays quiet). Even with fans flying, it's a quiet machine. So far, machine is over-kill for what I've been using it for. The prior HP laptop at 1/4th price was suitable for what I find myself doing. However, this purchase is part of a long-term investment into film making...

text:
I've got many laptops, and have had dozens of laptops in the past. I buy them often to keep on upgrading. This one has large memory and disk capacity and works great as advertised. However, there's a problem with it in that it will not wake up after sleeping. I've had it for a week and it has done this 3 times on me. You have to hard boot it - very annoying as I use it for 24 hour apps. Power settings are set to 'go to sleep' NEVER however, it goes to sleep and then won't wake up. I've read some possible fixes for this issue, but why, after spending nearly $2k on a laptop should I have to mess with BIOS and drivers. Disappointing . I should give it 1 star really because a laptop out of the box with these credentials should not have to be tweaked technically.
Updated after a month of use: I have spent hours updating BIOS and other drivers and trying to troubleshoot this laptop. It still - at least twice a week - will not wake up causing a hard reboot. For a laptop of this caliber, this is unacceptable.

I have software that I would expect to continue using that would need to be reloaded from a disk onto a new computer.  If I want to do that, I have to buy a peripheral unit. text:
The bottom line for this laptop is that it's powerful beast in a very small package. If you want a 13" laptop capable of running the latest games then it's a great option. It's not cheap, but contains some high quality components.

Read on for a lot more detail:

OVERALL CONSTRUCTION/BUILD

My first impression on picking up this laptop is how light it is for a gaming laptop. Sure it's only 13", but I was expecting it to be feel more dense than it does at just around 4.5 pounds. The overall quality of the case is high. I would say that it's not quite as nice as the machined aluminum of a Macbook Pro, but it is light years ahead of some of the cheap plastic-feel laptops I have tried out. It definitely feels 'high quality' in your hands.

The design features a glowing blue alien logo on the outside of the screen with a few glowing blue lines on a dark grey background. If you're looking for a "professional" looking laptop then this is probably not it, but considering it's branded with an alien theme - it's a lot more subtle than it could be. Personally I like the design.

SCREEN This display on this laptop is a gorgeous 3200x1800 screen, and it looks awesome. The Amazon listing says the resolution is 2560x1440 pixels, but this is definitely incorrect - the one I got runs at 3200x1800 out of the box. The screen is bright and clear, and everyting I've tried out has looked great on it. I'm not personally a big fan of touch screens on laptops, but I tried it out for a while and everything I messed around with worked well. One reason I don't like touchscreens much is that I hate putting blemishes on my beautiful screen from oils off of my fingers, but I have to admit that even after using the touchscreen for a while there isn't really any noticible smudging at all. One minor annoyance with the touchscreen is that flicking away a bit of dust on the screen ends up opening up menus or moving my cursor. Not a knock on this specific product at all, just a personal preference.

One thing to note is that with the 3200x1800 resolution on a 13" screen, this laptop scales up content through Windows settings by default. Through "Display" -> "Make text and other items larger or smaller" the default setting puts the scale up all the way. Most programs handle this scaling well, but it's possible that you will run into one that doesn't (like thie "Advance Product Registration" that pops up, the text is microscopic). This isn't a knock on the laptop, just the reality of running such a high resolution on a smaller screen.

KEYBOARD
The keyboard is surprisingly comfortable considering they had to cram it into a 13 inch laptop. The keys feel nice to the touch, and the space is used well. I'm especially happy to see that they found room for page up, page down, home, end, and delete keys. I use these keys often while programming, and I'm glad they're here. So far I've accidentally hit the page up/down keys a little too often, but I just need to get used to the keyboard. The palm rests are smooth and comfortable.

There are also lots of customizable keyboard backlight options if that's your thing.

TRACKPAD
The trackpad on this machine is not very good, it's the biggest negative in my experience with this product. It works alright I guess, but it's not anywhere near as smooth as the one on my Macbook Pro. Given that this is a only 13" laptop, the trackpad is a good size and fairly comfortable to use - but the texture of the pad is a little rougher than I'd like and this leads to scrolling that's just not completely smooth - the cursor tends to jump and skip a bit as you move it across the screen. Right-clicking is also a little finicky, sometimes I end up left-clicking when I intend to right-click. Gestures work fairly well with one major exception:

After setup I installed Chrome and started browsing around the web. The gesture behavior was extremely buggy in Chrome. It almost seemed completely random. Sometimes it would scroll correctly, sometimes it would snap the page to the top or bottom, it would often draw strange rectangles everywhere as I gestured. This behavior did NOT happen in Internet Explorer or Firefox, just Chrome. I tried to resolve it through driver updates but didn't have any luck. After research, it looks like the problem is with Chromium specifically, but I haven't been able to figure out a workaround. Here are two threads that have information on the topic:

https://productforums.google.com/forum/#!topic/chrome/BdaUw9boNSU
https://code.google.com/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=463350

As a result, I'm not able to use Chrome at all, which is a definite bummer because Chrome is my usual browser of choice. I've been using Firefox and the scrolling works very well, but I'm disappointed I can't use Chrome.

SPEAKERS
When I turned the volume all the way up on this laptop, I was honestly shocked at how loud these speakers are. It is MUCH louder than my 17" Macbook Pro. The quality is decent, it doesn't compare to a nice Sonos speaker or anything - but it's excellent for a 13" laptop. Not much bass, but boy are they loud.

GAMES
If you're buying this computer then it's highly likely that you're a gamer. I've tried it out on a bunch of different games, I'll talk about them here. The framerates are GENERAL ideas of the fps I was getting, obviously these fluctuate a lot during gameplay. I used MSI Afterburner to get the numbers.

Far Cry 4

I loaded up Far Cry 4 and it crashed immediately after launching! Bummer! I spent a while on this until I found a random forum post that said that MSI Afterburner causes Far Cry 4 to crash, and sure enough they were correct. Unfortunately that means that I don't have actual fps time data for Far Cry 4. I can tell you that it autodetected 1920x1080 on High, and this was running fairly well - but I scaled it back to Medium and the gameplay was a lot smoother. I'll stick with medium.

Fallout: New Vegas

Fallout: New Vegas autodetected 1280x720 on High quality, and it ran at a solid 60 fps. I scaled it up to 1920x1080 at Ultra quality and it ran between 40-60 fps.

Civilization V

Civilization V is a good example of what I mentioned earlier in the review: Some applications just aren't built to run at such high resolutions. Civ V autodetected 3200x1800 and the main menu was all weird, centered in between big black emptiness in the middle of the screen (Some people talkig about it here: http://steamcommunity.com/app/8930/discussions/0/864980734944032303/). The actual game worked ok though, but only ran at about 12 fps. I scaled the resolution down to 1920x1080 and it went up to about 20-22 fps. Frame rate isn't as important in an RTS as in an FPS, but there you go.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings

The Witcher 2 autodetected 3200x1800 at Low quality and ran at about 20 fps. I scaled it down to 1920x1080 and the framerate jumped to 35-50. I upped the quality from low to high and ended up with 22-32 frames per second. I'll also note that The Witcher 2 consistently crashed for me whenver I exited it, not sure why.

BENCHMARKS
If you're into benchmarks, I ran a few with this machine right out of the box. I didn't try to optimize these scores at all, they are just what I got with the vanilla machine:

3DMark
Sky Diver 1.0: 9209
Fire Strike 1.1: 3352

I also timed reboot, and it was just around 10 seconds. Very fast.

BATTERY

It's hard to give information about battery life because tasks vary so wildly, but I just had a battery charge last a little over 4 hours through some web browsing, video watching, and programming.

CONCLUSION

I decided to go with 5 stars for this laptop because I think for the correct customer it's an awesome product. I would have given it 4.5 stars if I could due to the lower-quality trackpad discussed above, but I don't feel it's worth taking off a full star for. I've put a lot of information in this review, and I hope it's enough to help you figure out if this is the right laptop for you. If there are any specific questions then leave them in the comments below and I will do my best to respond. I'll also be updating the review in the future as I use the laptop more and more. Best of luck making your decision!

text:
I really love the Advance 13-inch gaming laptop. Advance is a pricier, upgraded gaming line from FusionTech.

I bought a new Toshiba laptop last year, after years of living with a Gateway that was so bad it isn't even funny. The Toshiba laptop was a big upgrade for me, but it was nothing compared to this.

The design is unique and interesting and fun. It comes in a large box with an alien emblazoned on the top. When you open it, the laptop's unique design is the first thing you will notice. The top corners are slanted and this makes it a lot easier to manipulate and hold.

When you open the laptop, you will notice a small alien head centered above the keyboard. This is the power switch. Plug it in, the plug is highlighted with blue. Turn on the laptop, the keyboard has a blue backlight.

There is a facial recognition password program provided as a trial. It is pretty neat, but it is a trial and you will have to pay to make it permanent. The benefit of this is that it should work for all the programs on your computer. I am opting to not buy this, so I can't tell you how well that part works. But for the initial login, it works well. If it can't read your face, because of insufficient lighting, there is a traditional password backup.

Once I got going, the laptop pretty quickly and very easily transferred files and programs from my old Toshiba laptop through a Miscrosoft interface.

The screen quickly resembled my old screen in layout, making operation easy.

The big difference here is that the laptop has a touchscreen. Frankly, I am still getting used to this, but it does seem a lot easier to navigate and use. My husband has an Ipad and he is very familiar with this and frequently kids me about using the old trackpad.

The resolution of the screen is brilliant. It is clear and the colors are vivid, making my old laptop feel like it had a standard definition screen and this has a high-def.

For gaming, the Advance seems to be great. I play an online game and the graphics are much more vivid and interesting. The game also seems to move faster, given the faster processors on this laptop. My old laptop was designed more for personal and school use, so the processor was slower. Games were more sluggish and 'choppy'.

It is really a great laptop. Pricey, but worth it.

title_x: Good for the price, could use some tweaks. HUUUGE bezels that are empty.
text:
Great build quality, excellent value.

The FusionTech Worktop 7577 is a well-built mainstream gaming machine. From my use, I have noticed that my specific unit stays between 65 to 70 Celsius at load with the CPU and GPU, which is excellent for a gaming laptop, and better than competitors.

Pros:
+Excellent build quality, save for the display hinge/lid
+Easily accessible service manuals and easily accessible internals make this quite a repairable laptop
+Battery may be integrated, but it can be easily removed as needed, only one Phillips screw and some tabs holding the bottom casing in
+Uses standard FusionTech charging port
+HAS THUNDERBOLT 3!!!! This is a huge deal for when the GTX 1060 Max-Q starts to show its age. You can use eGPUs with it!
+1060 MaxQ at this price is incredible, a bit slower than the 1060 (10 to 12%), but may be overclocked as needed.
+The 256gb version uses a NVMe SSD, mine has speeds of about 3GB/s (gigabyte, not gigabit) read speed, and about 1GB/s write speed with Link State Power Management off.
+Has a 2.5" hard disk bay
+Battery life is actually quite good, up to 9 hours of use or so, especially if you peg the CPU to 800mhz
+IPS Display, 1080p display does NOT use PWM, at least according to reviews
+Has a fingerprint scanner
+Has a built in TPM, probably a firmware TPM, but is capable of BitLocker if you have Pro.
+CHEAP CHEAP CHEAP compared to the competition

Cons:
-Could definitely be a bit lighter, bezels are HUUUGE. It doesn't make much sense why, since most of the outer .75/1" lip is basically empty sans the ports.
-Top case/display leaves some durability out, fully plastic external construction. They could've at least used something akin to reinforced fiberglass/carbon fiber hybrid, although that's usually only for higher end devices. Display flexes, do not grab this computer by the display.
-Could use an extra 2 USB ports or even more with all the space on the case and on the back; weighs enough to which it's questionable as to why it doesn't have an optical disc drive
-Fairly middling colors on the display; light bleed near the webcam on a black screen.
-FusionTech warranty repairs sometimes can be harrowing, according to forums, if needed
-Red backlighting looks a bit gaudy, keys are red as well which has poor visibility with backlight off
-The maintenance hatch was not fully flush when I received the item. When I opened it to install a hard disk, and re-installed the cover, it was still uneven.
-Webcam looks like something on a $40 tablet from Gearbest

Other notes: Honestly, it's strange that FusionTech would put the Max-Q in this laptop but not in the ABC 15. FusionTech TB16 and other USB Power Delivery docks cannot provide power to the laptop, this is disabled. Part of this for the 240w TB16/TB15 is probably because this is a plain consumer/small business device. There's also a business version of this laptop under the Mercury name that is not available in the US.

text:
I got this laptop in January and have really enjoyed the features it offers, especially for my purchase price of about 890 USD.

The good...
The screen is good looking with dark darks and vibrant colors, and the inclusion of a fingerprint reader makes logging in a breeze... a natural extension of what we’ve come to expect from our phones. The keyboard deck is extremely rigid, sturdy with minimal flex and the keys themselves have decent travel and a satisfying actuation.
The speakers were a tad disappointing offering o.k. sound that lacks range, particularly on the low end... this is an important omission when the majority of people buying this product are looking for an emersive gaming experience. As I understand it, the previous generation offered a subwoofer... Music is a good experience though and movies sound good too. I also really appreciate the added battery life, just wish I could have my cake and eat it too.
The size of this laptop is really good. It is not a thin and light by any stretch but I think for the power the 1060 model offers, comparable offerings are much thicker.

Now onto the bad...
The screen, though pretty, makes darks in-game VERY dark, even with the brightest backlight setting. This isn’t a huge problem for me as I use an external monitor for gaming, but doing so on the go wouldn’t be my preferred method.
My second largest reservation is with the amount of system memory. If the model that offers 16gb of RAM had been in my price range I would have chosen it. Modern systems eat up resources and by the time you’ve opened 10 tabs on your favorite web browser while running background updates you will have used half of your available memory.
Battery life is pretty good. I haven’t taken time to measure the longevity, but for average users, students included, using a reasonable backlight setting, you can get several hours without a charge.
My final issue may be isolated for me... being a tech enthusiast, I have many spare hard drives. That being the case, I assumed adding a SATA drive into the available 2.5 inch space would be simple... boy was I wrong. It seems that the standard thickness for 2.5 inch drives has been abandoned for a thinner form-factor. An SSD fits with no issue, but I would have liked to put in a large capacity drive for games. This is something that should be revised for future models as it makes something that should be simple (for the consumer’s sake) unnecessarily complicated.
