text:
I bought this computer about a week ago now, and after uninstalling the FusionTech bloatware, it is a pretty nice computer! Needless to say, I bought it from *cough* Costco *cough* where its $750 right now. I would have bought it here, because otherwise, amazon has the best price I could find anywhere. If you don't have the Costco membership, it would probably be cheaper here, so it may be a toss-up price wise. anyway, let me tell you about my experience!
This computer is SOLID, as in its sturdy. The screen shows some flex, but not badly. The base is the best I have had in a laptop in quite a few years. The lone 256GB SSD leaves something to be desired, but is otherwise okay....sort of. The SSD is NVMe enabled, so the read/write is very fast and boot times are nearly non-existent.
8GB of ram seems to be more than enough for games like PUBG and TC's Rainbow Six Siege and it is definitely upgradable.
On the subject of upgradeability, it is very easy to access the internals of this machine, with the entire back plate coming off with only one screw. The ram can be upgraded to 32GB in a 2x16GB configuration at a max speed of 2666MHZ ram. The CPU and GPU are both soldered to the motherboard and cannot be removed, though you can take off the heatsink to re-paste them. There is a slot for a 2.5” drive; either an HDD or SSD via the SATA 3 connector.
On the note of aesthetics, the computer feels good, while perhaps a bit heavy at 6-ish pounds (3kg), but this isn’t a big deal. The keyboard is good enough for most people and is what I am writing this review with. It isn’t tactile, but nor is it too mushy for longer typing sessions. The backlight color is only capable of red lighting, but can be “off”, “dim”, or “bright”. There is no hotkey to turn off the trackpad, but you can set up the ‘settings’ to turn it off when you plug in a mouse, so it isn’t a deal-breaker. The screen looks really good for a laptop in this price range, with decent color accuracy and brightness. I think the brightest this display goes is 250 nits. Maybe too dim for some people, but I like it, because it helps curb eyestrain for longer usage cases. The bezels are not great, and the webcam is average.
Cooling performance is very good and I have had no thermal throttling under heavy extended stress tests. The i5-7300HQ reached a max of 85C and the 1060 a max of about 80C. The laptop feels responsive with the NVMe drive with little or no load times for most programs.
Gaming performance is arguably why you’re buying this laptop and although I haven’t had loads of time to test lots of games, I can give you two:
TC’s Rainbow Six Siege: mostly max settings at 1080p yields about 100FPS
PUBG: at medium-high I get a fairly consistent 75-85FPS with dips in cities to low 50’s. changing the settings to all medium and post FX to off I get lows in the low 60’s in cities. The only time the settings don’t help the below 60FPS are during parachuting and in the ‘war’ mode with lots of people.
I hear from a friend that battlefield 1, while it gets a good framerate, suffers from stuttering because the CPU is too slow. I would say that this is likely true as battlefield 1 is fairly CPU intensive. He also said that Fortnite’s Battle Royale mode gets about 65FPS on Epic settings.
Oh yes, Minecraft runs very well, even with shaders. Not sure about Crysis guys, sorry.
Overall, I would rate this laptop a solid 8 out of 10 for outright performance, a 7 of 10 for looks, a 6 of 10 for upgradeability, a 5 of 10 for battery life, 6 of 10 for portability and weight, 9 of ten for construction quality, and 7 of 10 for I/O.

title_x: Great price for a great laptop
text:
This review is purely based on my experience using this laptop for a month for work and a little bit of leisure around 12 hours a day, 7 days a week. I'll try to be as critical as I can since I believe this laptop deserves a very complete review. With that being said... I was surprised when I saw so many bad reviews at the time of purchase because the reviews on YouTube were a 10 out of 10 so I decided to jump in and try it the day they offered a $78.00 discount dropping the price to a total of $779.98 before taxes) because my old laptop was dying and I needed a replacement ASAP. I use it purely for work, college, social media, and a few games here and there. (I’m 23, working, in college, and definitely on a budget that only plays The Sims 4 and GTA V).

UNBOXING
A lot of people have commented that their unit came broken, already open and possibly refurbished but in my experience what I have received is brand new in a sealed box, inside an Amazon box with extra paper and plastic to protect the package. My unit was sold and fulfilled by Amazon. Also, no software errors or hardware issues whatsoever. It came as described at the time of purchase with 8GB of RAM, 512GB SSD, Intel Core i7-1065g7 CPU @ 1.30GHz 1.50 GHz, Windows 10, NVIDIA GeForce MX330 with 2GB GDDR5.

It has 1 HDMI port, 2 USB 3.0 ports (one on each side), 1 type C port, 1 audio jack, and 1 micro-SD port.

About the 512GB SSD I have to say that it’s actually 476.81GB (due to the discrepancy between the binary system and the manufactures count on capacity), with only 459GB usable, since 17.81GB are reserved for system and recovery purposes.

LOOK & FEEL AND USER EXPERIENCE
The computer looks very high-end with beautiful finishes in a light-silver color, however, when you touch it you can tell it feels cheaper than other models but feels good non the less, it's just the fact that it is made of a mix of plastic and a very thin layer of aluminum. It does feel very sturdy and doesn't flex or bend, at least in my experience. It is also very lightweight for a 15 inches laptop, which was really surprising. It feels like it’s going to take a few years before I see major scratches or surface damage, which I think is good.
It has a very bright full HD anti-glare monitor that honestly feels so big since there isn’t much frame space, which is something I love.

Once you open the laptop it turns on automatically and in less than 20 seconds, you’re on the login screen with everything fully loaded in the backend. It is THAT fast.

When the monitor opens, it has feet on the bottom and this raises the laptop up just a little bit in order to increase the airflow on the bottom. This, however, offers a choke point that causes the monitor to overheat sometimes, which shouldn’t happen too often if you use it to watch videos, check emails, and edit documents as I do. The fan doesn’t get loud, as a matter of fact in almost a month of using this laptop, I’ve never heard the fan make any type of sounds, ever. Also, the feet on the bottom might feel a little uncomfortable if try to use the unit on your lap., but that’s just me being picky.

KEYBOARD
The keyboard feels as soft as it can get for a laptop with this price and this many features. Definitely love the backlight keyboard and the button to adjust it (only two brightening options). The (FN) function keys’ imprint is very small so it might be a problem to read at first. Sometimes I have to get up close to fully recognize the key function. Once you get used to it shouldn’t be a problem.

The navigation keys are also very small but I got used to their positioning really quick. Also, the trackpad is very big in comparison to the body of the unit, which is something really good in my option.

FINGERPRINT READER
The fingerprint on the power bottom works decently. You definitely need to press a little bit and position your finger a certain way or it will give you a hard time reading it, but it hasn’t been an issue for me. I love the fact that it has it because it makes my login experience even faster.

WEBCAM, AUDIO, AND MICROPHONE
It has a pretty decent HD webcam that works just fine on Zoom or Microsoft Teams meetings. Very beautiful.

The audio quality could be better, there isn’t anything special about it. I would say it’s very standard. Doesn’t get too loud or crazy. You might think they would put it on the top but it’s actually on the bottom.

The microphone is also very standard, nothing really special. Could be improved but you can get your message across on a meeting or a recording without having to repeat yourself or scream.

FINAL THOUGHT
I think this is a really good laptop If you’re not a video/picture editor, programmer, or gamer. This unit gets the job done, looks, and feels smooth, and makes me feel very pleased with my purchase. I wanted to wait a whole month before submitting a review to make sure I got the best and the worst out of it to give an honest opinion on it. And I think this is one of the best out there for the price and also for a student or entrepreneur that isn’t looking for a computer with crazy features but just enough and a little bit more. Would 100% recommend it as a work from home type of computer and even as a back-to-school gift for your kids.

Hope this review covered as much info as you need and helps you decide whether this computer is what you’re looking for or not.

text:
I'm disappointed with the quality of this product and FusionTech's customer service. I bought my ABC 15 9560 from Microcenter with the top of the line specs - best processor, touch 4K, fingerprint scanner as I run a web design company and needed the power. The computer ran great, the screen quality is second to none, and heat management is pretty good. It fulfilled my needs as a web designer, running the whole adobe suite flawlessly and eating through 50+ open Chrome tabs.

It worked well for the first few months, but then all of a sudden, the rear screws holding the lower aluminium case to the upper carbon fiber stripped from their mountings. I looked in the computer body and found that the two aluminum anchors had completely broken away from the upper casing. This causes the case to separate every time the screen is opened, makes the screen "floppy" in open position and impacts both the power button (can be triggered when opening the screen) and charging port (loose in computer body). It is almost unusable, which is unacceptable for a $2,000+ machine that is integral to my business.

I don't aggressively open my screen. Additionally, the computer has been in a sleeve or on a desk its whole life.

FusionTech won't fix this problem. Even under warranty I was notified that this issue would not be covered (even as accidental damage and/or a manufacturing defect). I was quoted $200-400 to repair (the top carbon casing would need to be replaced as this is where the screws anchor into; the cost of this piece is $35-$50) this and a wait/repair time of about 2 weeks, from FusionTech.

The worst part is that this isn't an isolated incident. Two separate ABC products (one ABC13 and one ABC15, owners both friends/coworkers) experienced the same issue where the rear mounting anchors broke causing the issues mentioned above. If FusionTech is unable to remedy this, my company and I will need to simply cut or losses and switch over to another manufacturer.

Its real unfortunate that this is the situation, as the ABC 15 is probably one of the best windows laptops for creative professionals, but I can't recommend it due to my experience.

EDIT: This review was submitted to FusionTech.com, but rejected by them. It isn't displayed on their website.

text:
One Month Update 07/10/2017:
Everything still running very smoothly with this machine. Battery life just as good as when I first booted it up. Spotty wireless here and there is the only complaint I have for now. Still an excellent purchase.

Let me start by saying I was almost scared off of buying this laptop due to the abundance of bad reviews on the product page.
I was in the market for a reasonably thin, lightweight and good looking laptop, one that didn't scream: "look at me with my excessive red trim! I'm a gaming laptop and I want to make sure everyone knows it!" That being said, it needed to be able to play some of the latest titles on at least medium-low settings at 1080p. I needed something that would be equally at home in class taking notes and playing Battlefield 1 while I was shirking my responsibilities. After a lot of research, I just couldn't find any other laptop that hit that sweet spot between good looks, portability, and performance. And that's why I decided to pull the trigger on this one. I was expecting some headaches with it, but the fact that I'd bought it from Amazon and had legendary customer service available to me in the event of a less than optimal experience, I decided it'd be worth it.
The first thing I did as soon as I received the laptop was install all the latest drivers and remove some of the very minimal FusionTech bloatware that comes with the Signature Edition which I was lucky to receive. The device came with a fingerprint scanner which was also a nice surprise.
Now I've been using this laptop quite heavily for 3 days, playing Netflix, playing some Battlefield 1, running some benchmark tests and it's been performing as smoothly as I'd expect from a device at this price point. There have been no crashes or flickering at all, not while using Google Chrome or anything else. To me, that might be due to one or more of three reasons:
1) I got lucky and received one of the good products (unlikely, I have terrible luck)
2) FusionTech has sharpened up their game somewhat when it comes to QA (slightly more likely)
3) Some of the most common problems noted for this device have been due to driver issues that I resolved when I immediately installed the latest drivers available from FusionTech (most likely in my mind since it's been completely smooth sailing for me)

Now on to the actual review itself:

1) Build Quality: This laptop is supremely well built. You can feel the quality as soon as you take it out of the box. The laptop is sturdy and extremely well put together. It doesn’t quite match the build quality of the laptops Apple puts out, but for a Windows laptop, this, in my opinion, is the best you’re going to get.
It looks beautiful all around, the thing bezels look even better in real life, and the carbon fiber on the inside is a nice touch. It’s a unique choice that works out well, feels smooth to the touch and looks quite good.
The hinge is stiff and sturdy, and wobbles very little when using the touchscreen, which in my mind is another hallmark of excellent build quality.

2) Keyboard: The keyboard is perhaps the weakest part of this laptop. That’s not to say it isn’t good, but it’s not something that you particularly enjoy using. It gets the job done but no more. Perhaps regularly using a mechanical keyboard has spoiled me, but even as I’m writing this review on the ABC 15, I’m yearning to write it on my desktop with my mechanical keyboard instead.

3) Touchpad: The touchpad is good. If I’ve been spoiled in the past by using mechanical keyboards, the touchpad is the opposite situation. I had an ASUS N550J before this, and the touchpad on that meant you always needed to carry around an external mouse to use. With this, I feel no such need. It gets the job done, again not as good as the touchpad on a Mac, but for a Windows laptop, I’d place it somewhere along the top. The gestures are useful and you get used to utilizing them to get around quicker. It’s got a nice smooth feel to it with just a little bit of friction.

4) Audio: The audio as pointed out by many users is sub-par. I was expecting it to be absolutely horrible, but since I use headphones all the time anyway, I didn’t feel like it’d be a big deal. I was pleasantly surprised however. The audio quality, the bass, the mids the highs are actually quite decent. What’s bad is the actual volume. It doesn’t get very loud at all. Unless you’re in a quiet room, you’ll need to plug in some headphones.

5) The Screen: Absolutely gorgeous. The bezels somehow make it even better. This is my first 4k screen and it’s something you might take for granted once you’ve used it a bit, but as soon as I use the 1080p screen on my desktop, I immediately feel like something is missing. My desktop monitor has a 120Hz refresh rate and that’s awesome for gaming, a 4k screen is awesome for everything else. Both features are ones that you stop noticing after a while, until you use something that’s missing them, and then you realize how good you’ve had it. The color accuracy is spot on as well and is one of the minor reasons I bought this laptop.

6) Wireless: One word: “Meh”
I haven’t had any of the catastrophic problems some other reviewers have been reporting, but I wish the wireless were a little bit better. I’ll probably end up swapping out the Killer Wireless card for another one in the future, but it’s not a deal breaker by any means. Using the internet while paired with a Bluetooth device is a big no no. The internet slows to a crawl, interestingly I’ve had a similar problem with my old ASUS laptop as well. If that’s something that’s important to you, you might want to have an alternative wireless card ready to go before you get this laptop. Opening up the laptop is fairly easy, I’ve done it myself just to see if I could and changing out the wireless card shouldn’t be too much of a hassle, but for a device at this price point, really FusionTech should be doing much better.

7) Performance: Getting to the main reason you’d buy this instead of a MacBook. It is fast. If you’ve never used an SSD before, this will be a whole new world of fast for you. Some people have received a Samsung PCIe SSD, I only got a Toshiba PCIe SSD. This is apparently due to some supply issues and most people should assume that it’s the Toshiba SSD they’ll be getting, which is no slacker but not as good as the Samsung SSD. This is the main reason I bought the 256GB model, because I’ll end up getting the Samsung 960 Evo in the near future.
Day to day operations run very smooth, it’s pretty snappy and doesn’t give me any issues with web browsing, Netflix, word processing or any other meager task you throw at it.
For gaming, don’t expect it to run The Witcher 3 at Ultra, it won’t do that. What it will do is run most games at a smooth 60FPS on medium-low or sometimes even high settings at 1080p. Here’s some of my gaming experiences:
1) Overwatch: 60FPS at High
2) Battlefield: 60FPS at Medium. Occasional dips below 60FPS.
3) Battlefront: 60 FPS at Medium, some dips below 60 on High
4) FIFA 17: 50-60 FPS at 4k with everything maxed out.

8) Heat and Noise: With normal use, the fans won’t come on and it’ll be as silent and as cool as you’d like. I suspect it’s the Kaby Lake processors I can thank for that. While doing some gaming, the fans do ramp up, but it’s nothing too distracting, at least not for me. Heat seems to be dissipated quite well and I have no problem using it as a “laptop” while wearing shorts.

9) Battery Life: With a 4k screen at a comfortable brightness of around 40% brightness in a well-lit room, with the keyboard backlight on, I’m getting around 6-7 hours of non-gaming use. That includes web browsing, word processing and playing a bit of music now and again. That is not something I would have imagined getting 3 years ago from a laptop as powerful as this one.

All in all I have to say, this is an excellent computer. It’s got everything I, and I suspect most college students need and then some. It’s just a shame that some people will be put off it reading about some of the easily fixable issues that really should have been addressed from the start. I can only speak for my own experience, but I haven’t had any of the issues people have been describing.
I will be updating my review in a month or so, or sooner if something pops up that forces me to lower the rating on this review.

title_x: Good laptop for creative work and occasional gaming, with some minor caveats
text:
The Worktop 16 has a lot going for it, but a few shortcomings keep it from being perfect. The laptop’s strengths include a great screen, strong CPU performance, fast storage, and a responsive keyboard. However, the laptop isn’t ideal for gaming, its SD card reader is sluggish, and on my unit, the touchpad curls up at two corners. This laptop could be a great choice for content creators, but frequent gamers probably should look elsewhere.

The 3K-resolution screen is what really drew me to this laptop, and it doesn’t disappoint. Everything looks razor-sharp, colors are accurate, and the 16:10 aspect ratio is great for keeping extra toolbars/timeline on-screen while editing. The screen does have some backlight bleed along the top and bottom edges, but generally it shouldn’t be an issue unless you frequently work with very dark content.

Performance from the i7-11800H CPU is excellent, and this laptop handles everything I throw at it with ease. The 512GB NVMe SSD also does well, with read/write speeds around 3500/2500 MB/s, which is great for a PCIe 3.0-based drive. On the flip side, the laptop’s built-in SD card slot is a disappointment. For some reason, FusionTech installed an antiquated USB 2.0-based reader, which offers a maximum transfer rate of just 30 MB/s. If you frequently handle photos/videos by SD card, you’ll definitely want to use your own USB 3.x card reader instead of the laptop’s SD card slot.

When it comes to graphics performance, the 65W RTX 3050 GPU serves well for most creative applications but can feel underwhelming in video games. The screen’s native 3K resolution is a lot to ask of this lower-end GPU, so gamers would be best off connecting an external 1080p monitor for better results. On a positive note, the laptop’s GPU comes with Resizable BAR support already enabled, which provides a small boost in some games.

Build quality of the laptop is generally good, with one exception on the unit I received. On my laptop, the touchpad has a warping problem that makes it curl at the upper corners. The touchpad is attached by double-sided tape, which hasn’t been holding up over time, so I have to press the corners back down before using the laptop. I’m sure FusionTech would fix it under warranty, but it’s a mostly cosmetic issue that hasn’t yet annoyed me enough to ship the laptop in for service.

Touchpad aside, the rest of the hardware is solid. The keyboard feels responsive, with moderately-short travel, although its white-only backlighting could be brighter (lighting choices are dim, very dim, and off). The laptop offers decent upgrade potential, which is somewhat uncommon nowadays in mainstream consumer devices. RAM, SSD, and WiFi are provided as slotted cards for easy replacement (with a spare 2230 SSD heatsink included, which was a nice surprise).

Overall, the Worktop 16 is a powerful laptop that hits most of the right notes for content creation and general-purpose computing, but heavy gamers will likely want for better graphics performance. My only significant complaints are the outdated SD card reader and warped touchpad (the latter of which could be an isolated case on my unit). Four stars.

title_x: One of the best laptops I've ever owned ... but, there are issues
text:
I'll be honest -- I'm torn. One part of me loves this laptop so much. I currently have six laptops and this is one of my favorites. However, there are some issue that just prevent it from being a five-star product. It's possible that I've just gotten a "lemon," but I feel I need to let you know about them. But first, the pros ...

WHAT I LOVE:
-THE LOOKS: This thing looks sharp. It's very sleek and, for the power it has inside, it's pretty thin. It's not an ultralight, but to have an RTX card and 11th Gen CPU, it's quite small.
-THE POWER: The Intel 11800h is pretty amazing. The RTX 3050 and the RAM, not as much. I have two other pretty powerful laptops: a Gigabyte Aorus with an RTX 2060 and a 10750h CPU and an Acer Nitro with an RTX 3050 and a 10300h CPU. In Geekbench CPU testing, the Worktop blows them away. It's 130% faster than both the Aorus and Nitro. However, when I ran an OpenCL test, the Nitro actually performed better -- albeit by less than 1% -- than the Worktop, which seemed odd. When I looked at the specs on Geekbench, it showed the RAM only running at 1600MHz on the Worktop, but running at 2933 on the Nitro. I thought that perhaps it was running in only single channel, so I went and checked the specs with CPU-Z and HWInfo and they both confirmed that the laptop is only running at 1600Mhz in dual channel. CPU-Z lists the native speed as 800Mhz, which seems odd for DDR4. However, Windows shows it at 3200Mhz. So, there you go: Three different places show three different speeds. I have no idea why a side-by-side comparison in Geekbench would show the Worktop's RAM running at half the speed, but that's what it shows, and I have heard that Geekbench would be more likely to show the actual RAM speed, which makes sense considering the CPU blows the other laptops away, but overall tests falter. However, I will say that the internal SSD is quite snappy and startup times are less than 15 seconds for me, not including logging into Windows.
-THE SCREEN: This is, hands down, the best laptop display I have ever owned. Even though it only has a 60Hz refresh rate, it blows away my Aorus laptop, which refreshes at 240Hz. The colors are spot-on, which is great for the work I do in desktop publishing, and 300 nits is plenty bright enough indoors and outdoors on overcast or party cloudy days. Watching video or looking at photos on this is a pure joy.
-AUDIO: I know it seems odd to hear that for a laptop, but there's something very pleasing about the sound of the built-in speakers. They're not going to win any bass competitions, obviously, but the mid and high end frequencies are very clear and crisp, especially the highs. It is necessary, however, to keep the volume slider above 50% almost all the time as the levels are just too low below that.
-THE BATTERY: Of all the laptops I currently -- or have ever -- owned, this has the best battery life, by far. I've been averaging about 9 hours on a charge, which is pretty amazing, considering I usually multitask quite often, going between remote desktop software, Photoshop and several Chrome tabs.

WHAT I DON'T LIKE:
-INTERNAL BLUETOOTH: I don't know why, but anytime I use a Bluetooth device with this laptop, it freezes constantly. I thought it might be a problem with Windows 10, so I made sure all of my laptops were updated to Windows 10 and tried my Bluetooth mice on all devices. This Worktop is the only one that has this problem. I searched so many YouTube videos trying to fix the problem, but I gave up. I had to use an external dongle for my wireless devices, and that works flawlessly.
-FusionTech ISSUES!: After using this for about a week or so, I closed the lid and put it in my backpack to take to a friend's house ... about a 10-minute trip. By the time I arrived, my laptop bag was burning hot. I opened it up and a huge heatwave struck me in the face. I went to grab the laptop, and it was so hot that I couldn't even touch it. For some reason, the FusionTech software decided to run some kind of troubleshooting program while it was in sleep mode, and it got so hot that it nearly overheated, throttling my CPU and turning my laptop's case into a hotplate.
-BLOATWARE: There's way too much FusionTech software that comes with this. If you look in the FusionTech folder, there are tons of applications that seem unnecessary. There's also a preinstalled version of McAfee that behaves more like malware than an anti-virus program. I uninstalled it immediately. It even attaches itself to all of your web browsers without asking. Bad move, FusionTech.
-ERGONOMICS: The keyboard itself is fine and pretty easy to type on. The key travel is incredibly small, so if you're used to a mechanical keyboard, you probably won't like this. However, I do love the addition of the numpad as I need it for shortcuts in the software I use at work. My main issue with the design, however, is that my wrist constantly brushes against the touchpad, which causes my cursor to jump around and places it in odd positions while I type. Also, the fingerprint sensor is in an odd position at the top right. My Acer laptops have the sensor in the corner of the touchpad, which makes more sense, IMO.
-BATTERY DRAIN: I'm not sure what happened, but one night while using it, the battery drained from 100% to 0 overnight. When I went to check Windows to see what happened, it showed no applications running. I have no idea what happened. Maybe it was a Windows issue, but it's worth mentioning as it's never happened on my other laptops.

CONCLUSION:
I struggled on a star rating. I went back and forth between 4 and 5 stars so many times, it's not funny. Ultimately, I'm giving it 4 stars to allow some room for growth. I will continue to use this laptop and will see if these odd issues with battery drain, Bluetooth and overheating persist. If they seem like random anomalies or problems with Windows 10 itself, I will return and upgrade my review to 5 stars. For now, though, it's just a "great laptop." It's so close to being an "excellent laptop," but for me, it's just not there.

title_x: May be I expected too much!
text:
When I first saw the spec of this FusionTech laptop, I was thinking this one has all the things I find lacking in current HP HP Pavilion 15z. Thinks such like a slightly larger and better display screen @3K and support HDR, Thunderbolt 4 connection, a discrete video card for better 3D, even I am not a gamer. The tradeoffs are the display is not a touch screen, no mention of the keyboard is backlit (turn out it is) or not and Win 10 Home (it has since been corrected).

When I receive the unit, the first thing to feel is its weight. The packaging only contain the laptop, the AC adapter and a piece of disclosures, no other accessories nor manual. Although everything are online these days, something like keyboard functions that are unique to the laptop is still better to have a printed chart.

Even with a larger screen (16" vs 15.6"), this laptop is barely larger than the HP. Its weights however about half lb. heavier (about 4.4 lb vs 3.8 lb). While half lb may not sound much, it does made this laptop feels less portable.

Turning on this laptop I was surprised to find two things, the first is it came with Win 10 Pro instead of Win 10 Home. The original Amazon had the Win 10 Home in the title but Win 10 Pro in the description. It is good that it does came with Win 10 Pro. I think for the BitLocker encryption function alone, no laptop should ship with Win 10 Home anymore.

The second surprise was the keyboard is actually backlighted however, it is so dime that, even at brightest setting, it is still way too dim and it is actually worse than just paint white on black under low light condition. The keyboard are full size with numeric key pad and a large touch pad. The power button is at upper right and doubles as finger print reader. The keys while not the worst I have had on laptop, it has more of the rubbery feel than the HP.

I had high hope on the display as my desktop PC's monitor is HDR capable and I find the HP laptop's display wanting. I was very disappointed to find this FusionTech laptop's HDR is ONLY for video streaming, regular HDR and WCG apps are not supported, at lest not at default settings and I have not find way to get them on. As shown on the photo, side by side with the HP, one hardly notice much difference and the HP has much brighter backlighted keyboard.

As for performance, I was shocked to find the HP has higher Passmark Performance 10.1 than this FusionTech as the HP is AMD Ryzen 7 4700 based, although very capable should not have higher performance than this one as it does not have discrete video card and the CPU is a generation older. Upon looking at induvial scores, it seems this laptop only has significant lower 2D video and slightly lower memory score. This unit has significant higher CPU and 3D video scores as expected. On UserBenchmark, this one did get higher rating It seems it is Passmark's rating at fault. However, I was very disappointed to see such low score on 2D display as photo editing is important to me. More important than games in fact.

This laptop does not have an Ethernet port. Only WiFi. It uses Intel AX201 card that only support Intel chipset vs the Intel AX200 used by the HP. One would think Intel with Intel will give AX201 an edge, alas it is not so. Side by side on the same spot, using my desktop PC as test server with wired 2.5GbE to the WiFi 6E router (used as AP) testing 5GHz band with WPA3 security, this laptop's WiFi is sub par not only to the HP's AX200, it is also worse than my smartphone. Luckily if you are using this more like a desktop replacement than actual laptop, you can get an Ethernet to USB adapter that I have tested on the Thunderbolt 4 port to get 2.5Gbps no problem.

Speaking of Thunderbolt 4 port, while I don't have any devices to test it at 40Gbps, I did test it at 10Gbps without problem. The PD charging however, while a nice feature point on the spec, it has less practical use. The reason is this laptop is power hungry. The AC adapter came with it is 130W vs HP's 65W. I have not seen such high wattage AC adapter for years. While it is understandable the 3050 graphics chip is heavy power user, this made even 65W PD charger not able to keep up the usage and thus only able to charge while the laptop is not in use or switch to the IGP.

Speaking of high power usage, this one also generates a lot of the heat an fan noise when the 3050 is in use. the vents at back bottom can easily reach over 50 deg C. That also made this more of desktop replacement than something on your lap.

The NVME SSD that came with this laptop is quite good. Using Crystal DiskMark, it is on par with top PCIE3 NVMEs. While 16B RAM is more than enough for most people, for photo editing that keep several memory hog program running at same time, 32GB would have been better. Luckily, it is not difficult to upgrade the RAM.

This is one of the more service or upgrade friendly laptop on the market, all you need to do is unscrew the visible screws on the back. No hidden screws under rubber foot or label.

The first thing to note and not to my liking is the hinge design. I had more so many laptop got broken hinge broken with this type of design before made me fear this one would not last either.

There are TWO NVME slots in this laptop, however, one is limited to 2230 size, while the other can hold up to 2280 size. As one can see from the internal layout, it should not be that difficult to accommodate both for 2280 size, as the 2280 size NVMEs are more readily available and at lower per TB price. It is too bad the engineers decided to go with easy route. The good thing is heatsink are provided for both. A further good thing is the NVME came with the unit is 2230 in size. Although it was installed on the 2280 slot with adapter, it is easy to move it to the 2230 slot. This is important because the 2280 slow is PCIE4 ready vs the 2230 size is only PCIE3. I have test Samsung 980 Pro, a PCIE4 NVME on the 2280 slot and the speed while slightly lower than my desktop, it is excellent for the laptop.

Changing the memory is easy as the memory slots are next the NVMEs under the flaps.

I don't know if I can swap the AX201 WiFi card with AX210 as the HP would not and the current AX210 driver has WiFi6E WPA3 compatibility problem, so I probably will wait a little but that AX201's poor performance is a let down.

Now I like to talk about system recovery that I hope you never need to do as this FusionTech's system recovery was another down side of the laptop most people would not encounter. I normally not just back up but clone my working system NVME so that I have instant recovery. For this one because it is new, I only have the benchmark programs installed and I was trying to test out dual boot, bad idea. While the FusionTech BIOS is much better than HP, it only sees one Win boot manger instead of two (one for each NVME), on my desktop I can easily select which one to boot in the BIOS and not so in this laptop and to make it worse, after a few failed attempt, the boot manger on the original boot manager was ruined. First, I tried the FusionTech OS recovery assistant, no go. After a few unsuccessful trials, even the usual Win reset option is no long available.

I then tried using FusionTech's USB recovery imaging program, to download it from FusionTech's web site, you need the service tag of the laptop. If the tag does not match, the during boot, it will stop. This is nonsense logic, they can just check to see if it is FusionTech product, demanding exact service tag is not necessary and aggravate already bad situation worse. The FusionTech's web site's insurrections is also out of date or at least did not match my
BIOS. For example, there is NO legacy boot option on my BIOS.

To make dad thing even worse, the USB recovery program says HDD not found! Even when the BIOS has no difficulties to find both NVME and the USB. Makes one wonder whether FusionTech has fully test the recovery program or not.

Just when I was ready to gave up on FusionTech's recovery, I tried a last ditch boot and surprise, the Win reset option came back which was linked to FusionTech's own reset option and after several hours I finally got the laptop back to "new" condition. This recovery experience left me a rather low opinion on FusionTech's recovery utilities. If taking the recovery experience into consideration, I would only give this laptop a 3 stars instead of 4.

Overall, if you are looking for a decent laptop as desktop replacement with a decent size screen, playing some not too demanding games, this one is an ok option but probably not the best overall option.

title_x: Great Laptop if the Touchpad Worked
text:
This review is for the FusionTech Worktop 16 7610 16 Inch Thin Laptop (Intel Core i7-11800H, 16GB DDR4 RAM, 512GB SSD, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Graphics, Windows 10 Pro.

On paper, this was the best laptop that I could find for what I was looking for: 16" monitor, 16 GB RAM, minimum 512GB NVMe SSD, Thunderbolt, 10 key pad, and backlit keyboard. I was strongly leaning towards Windows 10 Pro (for various reasons), which this also happened to have.

I don't do any gaming, so even the on-die GPU would have been sufficient, however I do like having the RTX 3050 if I were ever to hook up to external displays for an overall two or three display setup (including the laptop's monitor). The 16" monitor is a big step up in screen area compared to the 15.6" monitor that I had been using for years. I also like that this monitor has no glare and an amazing 3072 x 1920 pixel resolution. The screen looked really good. I was ok with the screen only getting 300 nits bright, but I wouldn't want to consider anything lower.

This laptop was surprisingly small and light, especially given the monitor size. It was actually smaller in length, width, height, and weight than my 15.6" laptop, and that's even with this FusionTech's battery being double the capacity of my old laptop.

The physical sliding webcam shutter was a nice bonus, and I wish all laptops had a physical shutter or physical switch to shut off webcam.

The keyboard and touchpad both felt pretty good. The keys had decent feedback (for a laptop) and the touchpad is the largest that I have seen on a laptop. Unfortunately, the touchpad is where everything fell apart for this laptop. The touch pad gets jittery and stops responding. I originally purchased an open box from a local retail store that had this touchpad problem show up within just minutes of usage. The IT center at the store also had it show up for them within a few minutes as well. They did a full driver update, and it worked for about 20 minutes, turned off the laptop, and the next day about five minutes in and the touchpad started having the same issues again. I then tried the brand new floor model (running Windows 11 Home), and a couple minutes of using the trackpad had the issue on that one too. Even the manager came over and had the same issue. He said he has seen the issue before, and he said FusionTech's answer was to replace the motherboard (including the soldered on CPU). I found many reviews, posts, forums, even video posts, and tech channels all talking about the dreaded touchpad issue that plagues this laptop. The tech channels showed three solutions: change graphic hardware settings, place filler material between the battery and touchpad, or to solder on a grounding wire (voids warranty). Ultimately, it was the touchpad issues that had me decide to return the laptop and look for something else.

title_x: Beautiful red-lit keyboard, obnoxious blue charge light right next to it
text:
I really want to love this laptop. I want a computer I can relax and type with (aesthetics and feel), as well as one to play games and do some photo and video editing (processing power and storage), and this seemed like a good choice.

The keyboard is gorgeous with the red back light. It has a nice feel and it's easy to type with. The red logo on the back of the screen is stylish. The specs are nice, and I love SSD boot drive and the separate storage drive.

The screen bothers me. The moment I first opened the laptop I realized something was wrong, and it might irritate me into returning this. First, the screen is a bit smaller than advertised, it's closer to 15" instead. Second, the bezel (the frame around the screen) is pretty thick. I measured it and comparatively measured the image shown, and confirmed that the bezel in the image is a bit slimmer than the bezel on the actual laptop. The thicker bezel makes it look dated to me, since most modern monitors have thin bezels, so this feels like it's in the wrong decade. Maybe not a big deal to most people, but aesthetics were a big factor in the purchase of this laptop, so it bothers me.

Third, the charging cable has an obnoxious bright blue glow. One of the reasons I really love the red keyboard is because it's a nice dim light. Red is low frequency and easiest to work with in dim rooms, which I generally prefer. The bright blue charging cable cancels out that bonus feature. So either I keep my laptop plugged in and I'm annoyed by the light, or I unplug it and suffer the distraction, or more likely I'll need to cover it with something.

Fourth, when I finally turned on the laptop, it opened to an error screen. Weird, right? I haven't known brand new computers to open to a windows error.

So anyway, I worked around the initial screen error, covered the charging light with the instruction manual out of the box, restored the computer, and went through the setup process. Maybe I could get over the screen issues and fall in love with this thing, I hoped. Hasn't happened.

The first game I tried to install was a basic download-from-Amazon point-and-click adventure game, and it can't seem to install properly and run. Ridiculous.

The specs on this computer are nice in theory, but some things are just off about it. I went with this computer for the specs and the aesthetics, and unfortunately both seem to be falling short.

title_x: You. Yes you reading this. Do not buy this. Seriously.
text:
TL;DR I regret spend over a thousand dollars on this laptop. You probably will too. Do not buy this.

Heat: I knew going in that there were overheating issues so I purchased a cooling pad in advance. This was critical because the reviewers on here were not joking. This thing gets HOT. I don't mean it gets hot when you really work the GPU. I mean it gets hot leaving it idle for more than 5 minutes. No, you can't just leave a gap for air flow. You will burn yourself. It has to be on a cooling pad or have a fan actively blowing on it.

Battery life: As a direct result of the cooling pad needing to draw power 100% of the time the laptop is running, the battery life is a complete joke. I have to pack my charger literally everywhere I go.

Hardware defect #1: The internet connectivity goes down more than a "night shift" worker if you know what I mean. Turns out it is because of a power saving "feature" which you can eventually figure out how to turn off after hunting through a bunch of online forums, but why in the world are units being shipped like this?????

Hardware Defect #2: The left USB port connectivity suddenly started dropping out intermittently before eventually ceasing to connect altogether. After A LOT of troubleshooting I finally realized the issue was because a pin in the pin had not been bent up enough to make a solid connection. The first time I put a cable in, it slightly depressed the pin down and continued farther down each time thereafter.

Hardware Defect #3: In the bottom left corner of the screen, there is a defect which looks like a small, for lack of a better term, "burned" section of black pixels. It came out of the box like this but I put up with it because it wasn't that big a deal (because it was too small to raise a stink about) UNTIL

Hardware Defect #4: A vertical black "line" appeared suddenly last night. After going through all the normal troubleshooting (and then some) turns out it's a line of dead pixels and I need the entire display replaced.

Design Flaw: I realize you have to stand out, but having a central hinge in the middle looks cool but it causes way way too much stress on the case/display when you open and close it. title_x: Awesome laptop, multiple problems with hardware
text:
Let me start out saying this thing is awesome. Screen is huge and beautiful. core i7 processer runs everything I"ve thrown at it like a champ, including games on highest detail. Nvidia 650M is more than sufficient. Keyboard is nice and roomy, I love the number pad, Windows 8 takes a bit of getting used to, and is definately screams for a touchscreen, however it's fast and secure and easy to operate once you get the hang of it.
The only cons I can think of are: 1. Build materials seem a bit cheap 2. Battery is pathetic, but I wouldn't expect much more from a high performance machine. 3. Gets a bit hot when gaming, but I think that's the price you pay for performance. 4. I understood fully that this thing was heavy, and bulky when I purchased it, but it bears repeating. It's huge, and can be a pain to lug around! Overall I love this laptop.

But now I have to mention the multiple hardware problems I had, initially. I first bought this around Christmas. It started failing on me after the first week, refusing to boot windows. I contacted FusionTech tech support, who claimed it was some issue with the bios being locked and unchangeable. Most likely a faulty motherboard. I returned the laptop to Best Buy, and received the same model in replacement. A few months later, after the exchange period at best buy ran out, the NEW laptop started doing the exact same thing. Wouldn't boot to windows. Hours on the phone with FusionTech tech support, and they determined that i needed a replacement motherboard. Their policy is to give you one free 'on-site' repair, even with the basic warranty, so they sent a local FusionTech repairman to put in a new motherboard. After installing the new mb, problem seemed to be fixed, however my Nvidia card wouldn't work. (17Rse has dual video cards, intel integrated for the simple stuff, and nvidia for the heavy graphics. It was obvious that the intel was the only one working by the difference in performance of my games). It appeared that the new mb FusionTech sent me had a bad video card, and the local FusionTech service guy agreed.

I called FusionTech, and after another long diagnosis session over the phone, they determined the same. Problem is, they refused me another on-site repair, as it is their policy to only offer basic warranty holders one on-site repair. I understand this policy completely, except that the only reason a second repair was necessary was because THEY SENT A MB WITH A BAD VIDEO CARD!!!. I spent many more hours on the phone trying to convince the good folks at FusionTech in India that they should make an exception since the hardware they sent was faulty. They could care less. VERY FRUSTRATING!!! So, my two choices were send it back to the depot for repair (and wait a week), or pay the extra $50 or $75 to have the FusionTech repairman come back and repair on-site. I bit the bullet and paid the extra cash, which I think was ridiculous. This whole episode left a bad taste in my mouth to say the least.

Finally with a THIRD new MB installed, everything seemed to be working (I made the on-site repairman hang around a bit while I tested EVERY function and component of the laptop.) It's been roughly 9 months and I've had no further issues. The laptop is awesome. Fortunately for FusionTech, I have a long history, and many good experiences in the past with them, so I'm willing to let this one go.

It's reasonable to expect that any new piece of electronics will have some duds. That's just the way it is, but two duds from the same store, with the exact same problem? Maybe a bad batch? Overall, I don't regret the purchase at all because it's become such a great machine, once all the problems were ironed out.

text:
First, please be aware that Amazon often mixes reviews for various optional models on a single item’s page. That is the case with the reviews here.

THIS review is specifically for the FusionTech ABC 9700 17-inch Ultra High-Definition+ Touch Screen laptop with the 1Tb NVMe hard drive, the 6-cell (97 Watt-Hour) battery, the 130-Watt rapid charger, 10th Generation Intel Core i9-10885H processor, 32 Gb RAM, Qualcomm Killer AX500s DBS Wi-Fi module, Bluetooth 5.2, and the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 video graphics processor with 6Gb dedicated memory to supplement the built-in Intel UHD Graphics 630 CPU based graphics.

This is, by all measures, a top-of-the-line powerful, capable, and stylish laptop with excellent battery life, fast charging, and an amazingly sharp and bright display. Despite its slim and sleek profile, it is a workhorse with an amazingly large 17” screen in a package just a half inch deeper than my old HP 15.4-inch laptop and much thinner and lighter. Open, it has a handsome “carbon fiber” look keyboard platform, a huge touch-pad, and that stunning wide-viewing-angle 3840 X 2400 9.2 Megapixel screen with a minuscule .0954mm pixel pitch. Closed, it is all metal on the outside.

As I began to put it through its various usability tests, I found that the laptop was, as expected, amazingly fast and responsive. Cold boot times are on the order of 20-25 seconds from opening the lid (if using facial recognition sign on) and wake-up from sleep averages 7-9 seconds.

I configure the laptop to use three different sign-on schemes, PIN, fingerprint reader, and facial recognition. As expected, PIN works flawlessly every time but if it is a number only PIN, the lack of a dedicated number pad on the keyboard slows entry somewhat. FusionTech could perhaps have chosen to narrow the keys and relocate the two stereo speakers that flank the keyboard thereby gaining enough space for a number pad, but it would have required that the keyboard be compact instead of the comfortably large standard-size keys that are a joy to type on.

After configuring the fingerprint reader, it too flawlessly recognized my fingerprint quickly and reliably every time and rejected all other attempts at using the wrong fingerprint. It is, in this application a viable security method in my opinion. Lastly, I engaged the facial recognition feature of sign-in. This means that you will need to allow camera operation, so the typical piece of tape over the camera practiced by paranoid users will defeat this function. It is, by far, the fastest and easiest of the sign-in options and, like the fingerprint reader, accurate and reliable. I did a little testing whether it could be fooled by a good picture or a selfie on a large tablet, and it did not respond to those “hacks”, but like any security system, I’m sure it can be defeated with enough effort. Still, it worked perfectly for me scores of times using my actual face.

Once all the Windows set-up questions were completed, I began installing various programs and applications for my use. Since, like most modern “slim” laptops, this computer lacks a CD / DVD drive, I had to employ an external one to load some of my older applications. The laptop comes with a pair of USB 3.2 Gen 2, DisplayPort 1.4 (supporting up to HBR2), Thunderbolt 3 ports on each side, and using a USB C to USB A adapter, my old external drive was immediately recognized.

The ABC 17 came with some FusionTech applications pre-installed. Some may consider them as “bloat-ware,” although I found many of them useful. FusionTech’s Support Assistant, for instance, keeps drivers up to date and performs a “tune-up” on demand. Similarly, FusionTech Power Manager is very useful for customizing battery life. I recommend giving them a chance and deciding which ones are useful for you and removing the rest later.

During extensive use testing, I ran up against some limitations of the included Windows 10 Home operating system. Therefore, after a few weeks, I upgraded the OS to Windows 10 Pro using a complete reformat and clean install. This required that I re-visit the FusionTech support site and re-install some of the more useful FusionTech utilities and features, but I found the process to be smooth and trouble free. Once win 10 Pro was installed, I began to work the computer in earnest.

If you use very processor-intensive applications the two internal fans will spool up and can be somewhat noisy, but during typical use they rarely engage. During high resolution gaming, expect the fans to run continuously at varying speeds. Temperature control seems adequate to keep the outside of the laptop comfortably cool. For a slim laptop, the built-in speakers and two rear “subwoofer” ports provide remarkably good sound. The built-in sound card can drive a full multi-channel setup given the right external adapter and speakers.

The lack of a LAN port (RJ-45) was almost always compensated by the very capable and strong Wi-Fi adapter that connected almost instantly to either of my two home wireless networks whenever the computer was awakened. But, in the interest of running some file transfer tests across my LAN, to and from my NAS servers, I acquired an Anker 11-in-1 USB 3 hub that allows for a wired Ethernet connection (among many other options).

Using the Anker hub, and running many hours of tests, I discovered that the laptop’s built-in USB 3.2 ports can handle virtually any challenge at top speed. Not once did the laptop limit transfer speeds. Rather, the limits of the Gigabit LAN or the hardware of the various external drives I used determined maximum speeds. Additionally, the hub allowed me to use two external 1080p monitors, and although the ports are rated up to 4K, unfortunately I did not have any displays to test that with. The laptop easily supports external displays in “duplicate” or “extended desktop” modes.

Next, I ran the laptop on battery power alone during a routine day of authoring and browsing and emailing via the Wi-Fi connection. Battery life was exceptional despite purposely running the display at higher than recommended brightness. After nearly 7 hours of work with few interruptions the battery meter still read around 18%. Using the supplied 130-Watt charger, it recovered the full charge in just under two hours, which makes this one of the most portable and usable field machines I have ever used. My vehicle, which has a 110V outlet in the console and a built-in Wi-Fi hotspot make for an exceptionally productive mobile office using this computer.

When you first get started with this high-end laptop, you will undoubtedly find that some of the functions do not perform exactly the way you want them to. One of the most important is how the touch-pad responds to your touch. I need to say, unequivocally, that THIS laptop is NOT the one so many reviewers have panned for its touch-pad issues. First, there are many settings that can be applied to customize the touch-pad sensitivity, response, and functions. This touch-pad is glorious to use. It is big enough to allow for incredible pointing detail and can easily be set to move the cursor fully across the screen with a single swipe. It makes “Click and Drag” functions fast and simple. The touch-pad is rock solid, doesn’t move in its frame, is silent, and bulls-eye accurate. All the multiple finger gestures are supported and customizable. It works so well that I hardly, if ever, resort to the touch screen. There is, of course, an option to add an external mouse, and even a setting that allows you to have the built-in touch pad turn off when you connect the mouse so you can use the panel as a wrist rest without inadvertently moving the cursor.

If, while you are using this laptop, you find one of its functions annoying or imperfect, it’s my belief that buried somewhere in Windows or a FusionTech app, there’s a setting for it that will allow you to fine tune it to your liking. You just may have to hunt for it.

This is an ideal, fast, beautiful business / graphics laptop that will work at lightning speed to get your jobs done. It’s a high-rez, clear-screen gamer with a very fast and capable NVIDIA graphics adapter. It’s a looker, and easy to carry, charge, and use. Information storage and retrieval is virtually instant due to the fast i9 CPU and the extremely fast and huge NVMe drive. It is fast booting and runs most apps at blazing speeds.

But, I do have a few quibbles to comment on perhaps to prove that nothing is perfect.

First, for me, it’s a shame that such a powerful laptop comes with Win 10 Home, not Win 10 Pro. Since it is such a strong business machine, I would expect that it will be used in a domain environment. Win 10 Home does not support domains, nor do they allow remote access. You have to upgrade to Pro for $99 retail to fix that.

Next, there is an included USB 3 adapter to hook an external display and any standard USB-A cabled accessory, but it does not have a LAN port. Again, in business , you may want to hook to a wired network for internal security, and that requires a third party adapter. Both adapters I did try to use for this worked flawlessly and at full LAN speeds though.

The camera is weak. It only supports 1280 by 720 resolution, which given the exceptional graphics screen on this machine, is inadequate. It does work just fine for conferencing though.

Ergonomically, three things strike me as negatives. One, the case is actually hard to open, as it has no real grip point on the front to swing open the screen and it is stiff to open. Maybe it will loosen with time. Second, you cannot fold this back to use it as a tablet, despite the touch screen. To me, that is truly minor, but others may feel it is more important. Third, the front edge of the body where one naturally rests one’s hand when using the touch-pad is not rounded in any way. It is a sharply defined edge that eventually irritates the heel of your hand after hours of use. I started using an external mouse when I intended to work long hours on it.

Lastly, the computer comes with some “bloat-ware.” Some is from Microsoft, some is from FusionTech. Some of the included apps are actually useful, but I found some to be just a waste of storage space. Your needs may dictate that you will have to systematically remove some of these apps.

In conclusion, this is a fabulous high-end laptop. Comparing it to my brother’s premium Macbook Pro, it is very similar in performance and yet is considerably less expensive than the Mac. It is backed by what I consider to be an industry leader in support and service and backed by a very extensive support website. It never crashed, faltered, or failed to run anything I tasked it with. It has industry leading battery life and recharge times, and is satisfyingly fast.

As well as it performed, there is no way that my few negative points could add up to detract even a half a star from my unequivocal 5-star rating. If you need a monster laptop in a demure package with an all-day battery, this is your machine.

title_x: The value of this laptop comes from detail
text:
This ABC 17 is a system for a well-informed professional without much budget constraints. Such a person would value presentation, portability and pixel count over raw performance, but they also have enough computing needs to refuse to compromise too much on performance.
Value: If you just want to game on a laptop, you can get basically the same GPU of RTX 2060 and a better AMD cpu of Ryzen 4900hs from the ASUS Zephyrus G14. At $1400 as of this review, the Zephryrus is a far more attractive option based on the numbers. However, there are many details FusionTech put onto this laptop that makes it possibly worth the +$1000 premium (As of this review, the current generation ABC 17 can be as low as $2400 depending on where you look)
Screen: If you have good eyes and a need for screen pixel estate, the glossy 4K+ screen is absolutely gorgeous and can fit a ton of windows and spreadsheets when scaled to 100%. The touchscreen adds a way to efficiently interact with it. This screen is basically bezel-less, you get 17” of screen in a laptop the size of a 15” laptop, indeed I was able to fit this laptop in a bag compartment for 15” laptops only where my old 17” gaming laptop would definitely not fit. The high resolution and normal (I assume 60hz) refresh rate makes it a productivity machine, as opposed to gaming machines with lower resolution and higher refresh rates.
GPU: You can game with modern titles, but games would not necessarily be able to run at 4K and still get a good framerate. Compared to my 4 year old gaming laptop with an nVidia GTX 980M, the RTX 2060 max-q in the ABC offers basically the same performance and some new features in a much smaller package. And I know my GTX 980M struggled with games a lot, even at 1080p. The 2060 Max Q is considered “VR-ready” and most games developed for VR should be playable, however normal games with VR mode are more demanding and could struggle to run.
CPU: The only reason to choose Intel for this generation is if there are some Intel-specific features you need for your work, or if the rest of the laptop happens to be quite good as is the case here and you’re willing to compromise on the CPU. While by no means a slouch, you are not getting the best laptop CPU in terms of performance and efficiency. The Intel I9-10885H is worse than the AMD R9 4900HS in every way with higher power consumption and lower processing speed, the only exception being slightly better single thread performance - a small consolation in a world where developers are used to optimizing apps for multiple threads. A workload I use a lot is x264 video encoding. Measuring the power draw and frames processed over 12 hours, the i9 has double the efficiency as my 5 year old i7, but 20% less efficiency than my desktop ryzen 3900x. Less efficiency also means more heat: with ideal cooling conditions (a 50W box fan blowing on the laptop), the CPU was able to draw about 90W more power than idle.
As a system, the CPU+GPU combination was able to playback youtube 8K60 content with no stuttering.
Ports: I like the ports on this laptop, there are 4 thunderbolt/type C ports which serve to both transmit data and charge the laptop. A 130W usb C charger is included, you can also charge using a USB PD (Power Delivery) charger. This is exciting as it opens up the possibility of charging a full size gaming laptop from a USB C power bank via the PD protocol: My current on-the-go tablet, a Surface 3, was purchased entirely on the basis that at the time, it was the fastest windows powered x86 machine I could get that could be charged from a power bank.
Battery: A fully charged battery can last more than 3 hours of casual use, or 90 minutes with the CPU at 100%. My attempts to charge the ABC 17 from various power banks 10W-60W and prolong its runtime when not connected to mains, were met with limited success: Starting with both batteries at 100% hoping that the power bank would slow down the discharge rate, older power banks simply would not charge. Newer power banks would connect, but because type c to type c is non directional, the laptop would attempt to charge the power bank instead of letting the power bank charge it (there doesn’t seem to be a software switch to toggle direction of power). Finally, the PD power banks appeared to start charging the laptop after the laptop’s battery dropped below 80%.
Dongle: The laptop has only type C ports so regular peripherals will need to be connected via dongles or hubs. A basic HDMI+USBA dongle is included in the package. There are many dongles but I recommend getting one with full 4K 60hz video output and 100W PD, which allows you to charge the laptop through the dongle while freeing up the other ports for more dongles! A well-made single dongle will simultaneously: transfer 4K60 video signal to an external screen, copy files from external usb A hard disks and internal sd card readers at combined 200 megabytes/s, pipe in 900 megabits/s of internet upload/download, and power the laptop from an external PD power source
Longevity: This laptop includes the “FusionTech Power Manager” utility that allows you to limit charge to a number less than 100% if you keep your laptop plugged in all the time. Keeping batteries topped off at 100% is bad for longevity – I’ve experienced multiple battery failures on devices I need to leave plugged in 24/7. Capping charge at 60% will maximize battery longevity while 80% will give you a bit more flexibility if there is a power outage or if you need your laptop for an unplanned excursion. If you don’t know what percentage to use, you can leave Power Manager on auto or set it to one of several presets. The technology to limit charging has been around for ages, disappointingly not all manufacturers include this function. The ABC is also a model where you don’t have to worry about availability and instructions for replacing the battery.
Software: Windows Hello, using infrared facial recognition to unlock the PC, is a very convenient alternative to passwords. 365 days of McAfee LiveSafe are included although I have not had good experiences with McAfee antivirus in the past.
Keyboard: In exchange for the lack of a numpad, you get normal sized backlit keys and nice speakers on the sides of the keyboard. The way the Fn key works is interesting as an inversion of how Fn usually works: the F1/ F2… keys activate the Fn functions by default, if you want to input F4 you have to press Fn+F4. Commands like Alt+F4 still work as usual.
Condition: The specs and condition of my unit appeared to be as described and there was no malfunction or inaccuracy in any way.
Summary: If you know what you’re getting into, the current generation FusionTech ABC 17 is a quality asset to your professional or personal needs, engineered for the long haul. A pricey machine that maximizes the utility of a portable small size, the ABC 17 is capable of gaming but best used for productivity or entertainment where fine detail makes a difference.

text:
The FusionTech ABC 17 is probably one of the best, Windows based, personal laptop computers that you can buy, there are some many things that FusionTech did right with this generation of the ABC 17, and at the same time there are so many things that they missed and could have done much better.
Let me start by listing all the positives and the features I absolutely love about this model:

- Excellent build quality, the chases, the screen, the keyboard, everything is on a apple level of quality, if not even better in some cases, for example the chases feels heavier and more solid.
- Screen size and quality - yes, being able to fit a 17 inch screen in a 15 inch frame, sort of speak, is quite incredible, the screen is plenty bright with 400 nits, the resolution at 4K is good, but only if you are a content creator, about that a little bit more later, and last there is touch for those that like that feature on a laptop, personally I am not a fan.
- Top level CPU combined with a great nVidia RTX2060 MaxQ - now here we have indeed a great CPU represented by the Intel Core I9 10885H with 8 cores and 16 threads, this CPU can deliver a great productivity and is a very capable gaming chip as well. The RTX2060 MaxQ is also still a very good mobile GPU and is great for video rendering and games as well, but about that a bit later.
- Keyboard and touchpad - To me this keyboard and touchpad are one of the best I have used in the last few years, despite the fact that the keyboard is not full size with the numeric pad on the side, it is still very responsive and comfortable to type on, and the touchpad, well is huge and that is convenient. Previous years and versions had an issue with the touchpad being wobbly, but this later version is perfect.
- Four Thunderbolt 3 ports, an SD card and 3.5mm headphone jack on board, TB3 to HDMI and USB-A adapter in the package as well, great port selection and all you need for your content creation.
- 32GB Ram and 1TB fast Nvme of internal storage - top level components that can get you started with your content creation, video editing and everything else.
- Included separate fingerprint sensor for easy access and Windows Hello.

Negatives:

- The cooling system on board is not capable to effectively dissipate the temperatures produced by the CPU and the GPU - I was forced to disable the Turbo Boost in the bios in order to keep the temps in control, otherwise even the simple tasks were making the whole system heat up fast and the CPU temps were going over 100C almost all the time (and that is with 22-23C room temperature) causing the CPU to throttle. With the TB disabled, the temps were around 80C.
- 4K screen - While great for content creation and media consumption, pushing all those pixels can be challenging for the RTX2060 MaxQ, so gaming is almost impossible, unless you are willing to lower all game settings to the minimum possible. otherwise you are looking at 20-25 frames.
- Touch screen, maybe is just my personal preference, but not all laptops need to have touch, especially high-level production or gaming laptops.
- Battery life - obviously with such powerful components inside, the battery life is expected to be nothing amazing, but I was disappointed. Luckily most of the times I am not using the laptop plugged in as a desktop replacement work horse.
- Very expensive, and not only as a laptop, but computer in general. For the price of over $3K you can buy components to build an incredible desktop, even with the component crisis today, same goes for laptops, you can get a top level gaming laptop that can do everything you want.
- Having to use the included TB3 to HDMI adapter in order to output easily on a external screen.
- The included web camera on the screen doesn't match the price tag of the laptop, the quality is poor and for this price, it should have been at least a 2K camera with good quality.
- Because of the poor cooling solution, which btw even with repasting with good Thermal Grizzly past is not improving too much, you can really utilize the potential of all the top-level components.

Overall, despite of the high-quality components and a build quality, it’s really hard to recommend this laptop, I think for the price, you would have a lot more and better choices.

title_x: Good construction and quick booting. Fan runs a lot and needs more RAM.
text:
Light weight and portable laptop. Build quality is good overall but screen seems delicate. Integrated battery claims 9 hr life but more realistic expectation is about 5 at mid-high brightness. Plenty of USB ports, including USB C. You can charge thru USB C but it took longer in my experience.

8 GB RAM is not a lot but it does handle heavy CPU loads well. I have read that RAM is expandable on this model but I haven't installed more at time of writing. It will run small files on Solidworks or Excel easily but will stutter with large files as expected. Movie playback is smooth on main monitor and external monitor with/without desktop stretching. The fan runs a lot and will be audible in quiet spaces such as a library but is not disruptive. I hate the offset trackpad but others might not. Keyboard backlight has 3 settings (off, medium, max).

Speakers sound good but have no low end. Loud if desired. I recommend uninstalling FusionTech's proprietary audio software and indeed all of the FusionTech bloatware except for FusionTech updater. On a related note, it ran a BIOS update after about 20 hours of use so hopefully that was normal because otherwise it's unsettling.

I have not had any hardware or OS issues. On low quality, GTAV averages mid-upper 30's fps steady. Maxed out, Overwatch averages upper 40's fps with occasional dips to 30's. Lagspikes on all games if you use Gamebar. Keyboard response is good for gaming, not mushy at least for now.

The process of adding additional RAM and upgrading the SSD was easy, and after doing so, I am more than satisfied with the performance of this laptop and still managed to spend (barely) less than $1,000 total. I've also benchmarked it against other laptops at or near the $1000 price point and it consistently out performs the competition. I've decided to break my review into three sections: good, neutral, and bad to discuss the things I really like about it, the things I'm indifferent about, and the things I don't really like. Here we go:

Good:

CPU - no doubt the star of this laptop, the intel i7-9750h is a 6-core, 12-thread 2.6ghz base clock, 4.5ghz turbo workhorse of a laptop processor. It actually out-performs the newer i7-1065g7 and i7-10510u 10th gen CPUs that are commonly found in the newest laptops.

Dedicated GPU - the nvidia GTX 1050 graphics card really does perform quite well for a laptop that is not branded as a gaming laptop, I consistently get around 85 FPS. It also has 3GB of dedicated GDDR5.

IPS Screen - I have a couple of nags about the screen under the neutral section, but the IPS screen does produce a vibrant, crisp picture and the thin bezel is quite nice.

Light-weight - at first I wasn't completely sold on the magnesium alloy design because it felt more like plastic when compared to my previous aluminum laptop, but it quickly grew on me. It is very light weight, yet doesn't feel flimsy. Overall the built quality of this laptop is good.

USB-C charging - this is really nice to have and a nice step forward in standardizing laptop charging.

Back-lit keyboard - I often use my laptop in low-light environments so this is a must for me.

10-key number pad - this is nice to have and honestly impressive that they managed to include this on a smaller 15.6" design.

Neutral:

Battery life is around 4 - 5 hours. Not great, but not bad considering it's a 3-cell, 56wh battery driving a 6-core i7 and a GTX 1050. The battery can be upgraded to a 6-cell, 97wh battery, so that's worth consideration.

Memory - it comes with 8GB of DDR4 RAM, which is not bad, but not great by today's standards, fortunately, it's in a single module with a secondary, unoccupied slot, so buying and installing an additional RAM module is easy.

SSD - The SSD in this laptop is not great by today's standards either. It's not terrible, but 256gb is a bit small and the read / write speeds are nothing amazing. Of course, the importance of this completely depends on your use case. For example, I store a lot of data in cloud storage, so massive capacity is not that important to me. I also purchased the laptop with the intent to replace the SSD.

No touch screen - most modern FusionTech laptops have touch screen, but this one does not.

Screen resolution - this is kind of nitpicking, but it would be nice if this laptop supported higher screen resolutions on the internal display. The GTX 1050 is capable of outputting 4K (and greater).

Touchpad - could be bigger and smoother, but it works well enough and has all the expected multi-touch features. I use a wireless mouse most of the time so I don't really care about the touchpad.

Bad:

No Ethernet port - I work as a network technician and often have to plug network cables into my laptop to test and troubleshoot. I have a USB-C to Ethernet adapter that works fine with the laptop, but it's just a pain to have to remember to carry it around when I need it.

Cooling / Thermal - The laptop can get very hot during extended periods of performance-heavy use.

Great machine, but NEVER buy one that has to go back to FusionTech just to replace the battery.
